articles.title: India, UK to exchange tariff usage data under trade agreement - Livemint
articles.summary: India, UK to exchange tariff usage data under trade agreement  Livemint
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: India and the United Kingdom on Monday agreed to exchange annual data on businesses' utilisation of preferential tariffs under their Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), the commerce & industry ministry said in a statement. The two sides agreed to establish committees, working groups and government-to-government contact points to ensure the smooth implementation of the trade pact, it added.
The decision was taken at the 16th meeting of the India-UK Joint Economic and Trade Committee (JETCO) in New Delhi, co-chaired by commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal and UK secretary of state for business, innovation, science and trade Jonathan Reynolds, the ministry said in a joint statement.
Under the arrangement, the two countries will begin exchanging data one year after CETA came into force on 15 July 2026, including information on how frequently businesses claim lower tariffs available under the agreement. The exercise will also incorporate feedback from businesses on implementation challenges and areas requiring further support.
"We agreed that we will exchange data annually starting one year after the date of entry into force of the CETA on how businesses are using the agreement," the joint statement said.
The two sides said the mechanism would help identify priorities and enable more companies, particularly small and medium-sized businesses, to benefit from the agreement. The ministers welcomed the cooperation that had helped resolve issues during the initial implementation phase and asked officials to address any emerging challenges quickly.
The meeting marked the first JETCO since negotiations for CETA began in January 2022. Both countries reviewed progress since the agreement entered into force and discussed priorities for the coming year.
According to the joint statement, Indian exporters dispatched more than 50 consignments to the UK on the day the agreement entered into force, covering products such as smartphones, electrical and mechanical machinery, including turbojets, gold jewellery, ready-made garments, woollen yarn, tea and coffee.
The first shipment of Joha rice from Assam to the UK also took place, marking the first export of the distinctive regional variety to the British market.
The first certificates of origin under CETA were issued through India's eCoO 2.0 platform on a self-certification basis, facilitating exporters' access to preferential tariff treatment.
On the UK side, the first tariff-free Scottish salmon reached India within a fortnight of the agreement entering into force, with several thousand kilograms exported since then.
Scotch whisky has also entered the Indian market with reduced tariffs, while the first cars exported under the tariff-rate quota have cleared customs and been imported into India, the statement said.
Beyond merchandise trade, the two countries agreed to deepen cooperation in services, innovation, government procurement, science and technology, and gender-related areas, alongside greater business-to-business engagement and regional partnerships.
The ministers also welcomed the India-UK Science and Innovation Council meeting and the Innovation Roundtable, held on Monday, noting their role in connecting businesses, investors and researchers and accelerating the commercialisation of new technologies.
The JETCO meeting coincided with a visit by seven mayors and a combined authority leader from the North of England, alongside broader engagements involving government representatives, businesses, universities, innovators and regional leaders.
Both sides agreed to continue gathering feedback from businesses, industry associations, export promotion bodies and other stakeholders to identify and address implementation issues under CETA.
The ministers also supported continued visits by high-level delegations to sustain engagement between the two countries.
The 17th meeting of JETCO will be held in the United Kingdom in 2027, the statement said.

articles.title: US tariffs accelerate global trade realignment: How India’s FTAs could boost GDP - Livemint
articles.summary: US tariffs accelerate global trade realignment: How India’s FTAs could boost GDP  Livemint
articles.full_text:
India’s expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs) could add around $140 billion to its gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 and increase exports by 6.2%, according to a report by Bloomberg Economics.
The report said the agreements could help India access new markets, lower import costs, attract foreign direct investment (FDI) and improve productivity as countries increasingly diversify supply chains and seek preferential access to overseas markets.
“Using a large-scale model of the global economy developed by the World Trade Organisation, we estimate these agreements could add about $140 billion to India’s GDP in 2035, opening new markets, cutting import costs, fostering foreign direct investment and lifting productivity,” said the Bloomberg report.
“We also consider two scenarios that could amplify the gains: realising further productivity benefits from a decade of reforms to strengthen manufacturing competitiveness, and enacting policies that help underemployed agricultural workers transition into manufacturing and services,” the report added.
The expansion of India’s trade network comes as rising US tariffs reshape global trade flows. Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, the United States has increased tariffs on several trading partners and product categories.
According to Bloomberg Economics, the average US tariff rate stood at 10.7% in August, compared with 2.3% in 2024. The increase reflected sector-specific duties, particularly on automobiles and metals, as well as country-specific levies.
The report said tariffs at these levels could reduce US imports of goods by around 15% compared with the previous regime. Further increases remain possible amid continuing tariff threats and investigations.
In response, economies are seeking to diversify their trade relationships and accelerate negotiations with new partners, creating opportunities for countries that can secure preferential market access.
India expands trade partnerships across major markets
India has accelerated its FTA programme after years of relative caution. During 2025-26, agreements with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), the United Kingdom and Oman entered into force, adding to trade agreements with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022.
India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded negotiations on a trade agreement with the European Union. New Delhi is pursuing additional partnerships, including with the Eurasian Economic Union, and has sought an agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council.
Other major economies are following a similar approach. The European Union has signed new or updated agreements with Mercosur and Mexico and concluded negotiations with Indonesia, India and Australia. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China signed an upgraded free trade agreement in October 2025, while Canada has also pursued several trade agreements.
US-India trade negotiations remain important
Despite expanding its trade links elsewhere, India has continued efforts to deepen economic ties with the United States.
President Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced plans for a bilateral trade agreement in February 2025. However, negotiations have taken place against a backdrop of tariff tensions.
In the second half of 2025, India faced some of the highest additional US tariffs among its major trading partners after Washington imposed a 25% reciprocal tariff and an additional 25% duty on purchases of Russian oil.
Bloomberg Economics’ estimates suggest that India’s expanding trade agreements could support long-term growth by improving market access and strengthening its position in global supply chains. The extent of the benefits will also depend on domestic reforms, manufacturing competitiveness and the ability to shift workers into higher-productivity sectors.

articles.title: 'FTAs can add $170 billion to India's GDP by 2035, cushion US tariffs' - Business Standard
articles.summary: 'FTAs can add $170 billion to India's GDP by 2035, cushion US tariffs'  Business Standard
articles.full_text:
'FTAs can add $170 billion to India's GDP by 2035, cushion US tariffs'
Bloomberg Economics estimates that India's expanding trade agreements could lift GDP by up to 2.1 per cent by 2035, while stronger exports elsewhere help offset US tariffs
Listen to This Article
India’s expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs) could add $140-170 billion to its GDP by 2035, according to a report released by Bloomberg Economics on Monday.
“Our analysis suggests FTAs already in force should raise India’s GDP by 1.2 per cent by 2035 relative to baseline, rising to 1.7 per cent if the EU (European Union) and New Zealand agreements are implemented from 2027, a gain of about $140 billion at constant 2025 US dollars,” the report said.
Bloomberg Economics further said a US deal would add 0.2 percentage points, and if negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Israel conclude over the next few years, the gain could rise by another 0.2 percentage points, leaving GDP 2.1 per cent higher (about $170 billion) by 2035.
The report said the Indian economy is well placed to absorb disruptions from the imposition of American tariffs, as expanding free trade partnerships aid the discovery of new markets, foreign direct investment and productivity gains, while global capital flows become more concentrated.
Bloomberg Economics estimated that the average tariff on Indian goods sold to the US has risen to 11.6 per cent from 2.4 per cent in 2024. “By 2035, we estimate the tariffs will cut Indian goods exports to the US by about one-fifth. But the hit to India’s economy should be limited. Less than 2 per cent of its output relies on US markets, and stronger exports elsewhere should cushion the blow. We estimate the effect on gross domestic product will be negligible,” the report said.
Also Read
Facing such uncertainty in its single largest export destination amid supply chain disruptions from the West Asian conflict, India is in negotiations with at least eight to nine more groups of countries and individual nations that together account for another $15 trillion of GDP, according to Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal. India has concluded nine free trade agreements (FTAs) with 38 developed countries in the past four and a half years. These nine agreements cover economies with a combined GDP of $60 trillion and 38 developed countries, Goyal said earlier.
The report projected India’s growth rates for calendar years 2026 and 2027 at 6.9 per cent and 7.4 per cent, respectively. Inflation is projected to rise from 2.2 per cent in 2025 to 4.5 per cent in 2026 and 5.3 per cent in 2027. The central bank's repo rate is forecast at 5.50 per cent for 2026 and 5.75 per cent in 2027, from 5.25 per cent in 2025.
The report further forecast that trade volumes, including imports, would rise even faster on completion of such agreements, with a rise of around 10 per cent by 2035 over 2024. “Imports would also climb as households and businesses gain access to new products and services, and manufacturers become more integrated into global value chains,” the report said.
However, the report noted that global capital flows are becoming more concentrated and more political, with flows between rival nations estimated to be 40 per cent lower than between allies, as capital zeroes in on artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductors. The report said AI could boost India's GDP growth by 0.4–0.9 percentage points annually through higher factor productivity.

articles.title: FTAs may add $140bn to India GDP by 2035, lift exports 6.2%: Bloomberg Economics - Livemint
articles.summary: FTAs may add $140bn to India GDP by 2035, lift exports 6.2%: Bloomberg Economics  Livemint
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: India's free trade agreements (FTAs) already in force, along with those agreed with the European Union (EU) and New Zealand, could add about $140 billion to the country's gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035, lifting economic output by 1.7% and export volumes by 6.2% compared with a baseline without the trade deals, according to a Bloomberg Economics report.
The October 2026 report, titled Silicon, Steel and Statecraft: New Economic Thinking for the New Economy Forum said the projected gain assumes that the agreements with the EU and New Zealand are implemented from 2027. The $140 billion estimate is expressed in constant 2025 US dollars.
The gains could increase to about $170 billion, or 2.1% of GDP, by 2035 if India reaches an interim trade agreement with the US and concludes ongoing negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Israel over the next few years, the report estimated.
According to Bloomberg Economics, FTAs already in force could increase India's GDP by 1.2% and export volumes by 4% by 2035, compared with the baseline. The addition of the EU and New Zealand agreements would increase the estimated gains to 1.7% and 6.2%, respectively.
A proposed interim agreement with the US could add another 0.2 percentage point to GDP gains, taking the total to 1.9%, while export volumes could increase by 7.8% compared with the baseline. The conclusion of negotiations with the EAEU, GCC and Israel could raise the projected GDP gain to 2.1% and export volumes to 9.2%.
The estimates are based on a computable general equilibrium model developed by the World Trade Organization. The report's baseline assumes that US tariffs remain at their 2024 levels and none of the trade agreements are implemented.
Bloomberg Economics said that the average US tariff on Indian goods had increased to 11.6% in August 2026 from 2.4% in 2024. It estimated that tariffs at these levels would reduce Indian goods exports to the US by about one-fifth by 2035.
However, the report estimated that the impact on India's overall GDP would be negligible, as less than 2% of the country's output depends on US markets and stronger exports elsewhere could cushion the impact.
The report noted that the average US tariff rate across trading partners stood at 10.7% in August, compared with 2.3% in 2024. Tariffs at this level could reduce US goods imports by roughly 15% compared with the previous regime.
The report said that agreements with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), the UK and Oman entered into force during 2025-26, adding to agreements with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022. India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded negotiations with the EU.
Bloomberg Economics modelled the impact of these agreements through changes in bilateral tariffs, reductions in non-tariff barriers and productivity gains associated with higher foreign direct investment.
For its calculations, the report assumed that India's trade partners eliminate tariffs on Indian goods in the first year, while India eliminates tariffs on industrial products and halves tariffs on agricultural products over a phased implementation period.
It also assumed that the cost of non-tariff measures on goods and services declines gradually by 25% over 15 years, alongside additional reductions in barriers affecting services.
The model incorporated investment commitments of $100 billion over 15 years under the EFTA agreement, of which roughly $35 billion was expected to be additional, and $20 billion under the New Zealand agreement, almost all of which was expected to be additional.
Beyond trade agreements, the report examined how domestic reforms could increase India's economic gains.
It estimated that a further improvement in manufacturing efficiency, modelled as a roughly 2% reduction in production costs, could add about 0.5 percentage point to GDP gains and roughly 1 percentage point to export gains by 2035.
The report also highlighted the potential benefits of moving workers from agriculture into manufacturing and services. More than 40% of India's workforce remains in agriculture, with high underemployment, it said.
A scenario involving higher agricultural productivity, phased in over a decade and allowing workers to move into manufacturing and services, could add about 2 percentage points to GDP gains and slightly more than 1 percentage point to export growth.
Bloomberg Economics said that realising the benefits of FTAs would require effective implementation, continued domestic reforms, reliable access to energy, critical minerals and advanced technologies, and measures to unlock the potential of India's workforce.

articles.title: India–EU FTA could strengthen Czech investment and manufacturing ties - Maritime Gateway
articles.summary: India–EU FTA could strengthen Czech investment and manufacturing ties  Maritime Gateway
articles.full_text:
Summary
Czech companies are seeking joint ventures, investment and technology partnerships in India, with the India–EU trade agreement expected to support deeper commercial ties. Czech minister Karel Havlíček outlined opportunities in engineering, construction, energy and transport during a business forum in New Delhi. The agreement is not yet in force.
Czech delegation looks beyond export sales
The India–EU FTA could create opportunities for Czech investment and joint ventures in India, according to Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Addressing the CII-organised India–Czech Republic Business Forum in New Delhi on 12 October, Havlíček said Czech businesses were interested in establishing partnerships and investing locally alongside their export activities.
He identified construction, energy, transport and research and development as areas for cooperation. He also highlighted Czechia’s engineering capabilities, including aircraft manufacturing.
The minister linked the delegation’s interest in local partnerships with India’s manufacturing strategy. His remarks describe prospective business opportunities, rather than a quantified investment commitment or a confirmed portfolio of new projects.
Business mission covers three Indian centres
The forum forms part of a Czech business mission scheduled for 12–15 October, covering Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.
Ahead of the visit, the Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade said the mission would support companies entering the Indian market and those seeking to expand existing operations.
The programme also included a planned roundtable with Invest India focused on developing bilateral investment opportunities. Direct business contacts and meetings were identified as important elements of the delegation’s approach.
The mission places the minister’s comments within a broader effort to develop commercial relationships. For participating companies, the immediate focus is identifying partners and market opportunities while the trade agreement progresses through its approval process.
The visit’s stated objectives combine market entry, business expansion and investment cooperation, extending the engagement beyond the promotion of finished-product exports alone.
Negotiations concluded, implementation still pending
India and the European Union concluded FTA negotiations on 27 January 2026. The European Commission subsequently put forward a proposal for a Council decision authorising signature.
Negotiating an agreement, signing it and bringing it into force are separate stages. The EU process requires the relevant Council decisions and European Parliament consent, while India must also complete its approval requirements.
Consequently, the agreement’s tariff preferences should be understood as forthcoming provisions, rather than benefits already available to shipments.
The talks began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and resumed in 2022. Separate negotiations on investment protection and geographical indications were also launched alongside the renewed FTA process.
That distinction is relevant to the investment discussion: the trade agreement and the separate investment protection negotiations address related but different aspects of the commercial relationship.
Industrial tariff reductions underpin the opportunity
The negotiated agreement envisages eliminating or reducing tariffs on 96.6% of EU goods exports to India by value. The European Commission estimates eventual annual duty savings of approximately €4 billion for European products.
Industrial goods feature prominently. Tariffs on machinery, chemicals and pharmaceuticals are to be mostly eliminated, while automobile and component provisions include phased reductions.
These changes provide a commercial backdrop to Czech interest in engineering and industrial cooperation. Lower trade barriers could support cross-border equipment and component supply, although individual benefits will depend on product coverage and implementation schedules.
The agreement also includes provisions on intellectual property and services, including maritime transport. Such commitments extend its scope beyond merchandise tariffs and could support businesses combining technology, equipment and services.
The Commission’s projections concern the overall EU–India relationship; they do not establish a specific increase in Czech exports or investment.
Indian exporters also stand to gain
The agreement provides reciprocal opportunities for Indian businesses. India’s commerce ministry says more than 99% of Indian exports by trade value will gain preferential access to the EU.
Engineering goods, textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, marine products and other labour-intensive sectors are among the areas identified for improved access.
The framework also covers rules of origin, customs and trade facilitation, regulatory cooperation and technical barriers to trade. These provisions matter to manufacturers seeking to build supply relationships across the two markets.
For ports, freight forwarders and logistics providers, any resulting expansion in industrial trade could create additional demand for cargo movement. Its scale will depend on implementation and actual business decisions.
The Czech delegation’s engagement therefore represents an effort to develop partnerships ahead of the agreement’s application, with investment and manufacturing cooperation central to the discussion.
FAQs
What opportunities are Czech companies exploring?
Joint ventures, investment and cooperation in engineering, construction, energy, transport and research and development.
Who outlined these opportunities?
Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Is the India–EU FTA already in force?
No. Negotiations have concluded, but the agreement must complete signature and approval procedures before taking effect.
Were specific Czech investment commitments announced?
The reported remarks did not provide a quantified investment package.
How could Indian exporters benefit?
The agreement envisages preferential EU market access across a broad range of Indian exports, subject to its provisions and implementation.

articles.title: India-Chile trade negotiations: A quiet and strategic deal beyond tariffs - The Economic Times
articles.summary: India-Chile trade negotiations: A quiet and strategic deal beyond tariffs  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The India-Chile trade relationship is not a new one. The two countries signed a PTA in 2006, which was expanded in 2016 to cover nearly 1,800 tariff lines. That arrangement reduced tariffs on select goods and widened market access but remained limited in scope. Further, to enhance economic integration and cooperation, in May 2025, both countries signed a framework agreement for CEPA, which would include several sectors, including digital services, investment promotion and cooperation, MSMEs, critical minerals, etc.
Though trade between the two nations has grown steadily, it has remained relatively small compared to other trading partners. Exports to Chile account for just 0.2-0.3% of India’s export basket, while Chile exports around 2-3% of its total exports to India by value. Chile’s exports are very concentrated, with China occupying around 40% of its exports. Chile’s export basket to India is dominated by copper and related minerals, alongside chemicals and some agricultural products. India, in turn, exports pharmaceuticals, automobiles, particularly two- and three-wheelers, textiles, and engineering goods. Though this relationship may not be trade-heavy, it is trade-compatible. And in the era of energy transition, that compatibility requires a dimension: improved market access with supply-chain resilience.
Chile holds some of the world’s largest lithium reserves and is a major global producer of copper. These are not ordinary commodities; they are critical inputs for industry and the global net-carbon neutrality goals. Lithium is central to electric vehicle (EV) batteries, grid storage systems, and renewable energy apparatus. Copper is also indispensable for power transmission, EV charging infrastructure, and the expansion of electricity grids. In a rapidly changing world, metal and mineral security has become synonymous with industrial security.
In this respect, India’s ambitions are clear. It aims to scale up EV adoption, expand solar and wind capacity, build domestic battery manufacturing under production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes, and reduce import dependence in critical sectors. However, secure, sustainable, and diversified access to critical minerals and metals, such as lithium and copper, is essential for realising these ambitions. At present, global mining, processing, and refining capacities for many critical minerals are highly concentrated, creating vulnerabilities in supply chains. For India, expanding partnerships with resource-rich countries like Chile is not only about lowering tariffs; it is also about building long-term supply chain resilience amid a fragmenting world order.
Additionally, there is a larger geopolitical context. Much of the recent global discourse on critical minerals has been framed through strategic competition among major powers, like China and the US. India-Chile cooperation offers a different model, which is rooted in Global South collaboration rather than bloc politics. It demonstrates that strategic supply chains can be diversified through pragmatic economic partnerships, without being a part of geopolitical blocs.
Ultimately, the success of the India-Chile agreement will depend on how negotiators treat it. Though lowering or eliminating the tariff and non-tariff barriers for the merchandise trade may bring welfare effects for both countries, a strategic expansion rather than a conventional one would anchor a long-term industrial partnership.
If designed with foresight, integrating trade, minerals, investment, technology, and sustainability, it could present a model for sustainable economic partnership for the Global South also. The scope of the agreement, therefore, should not remain partial. It should become strategic.
Dr. Badri Narayanan Gopalakrishnan, PhD is the Founder of Infinite Sum Modelling. Himanshu Jaiswal is Research Fellow, Infisum Modeling.

articles.title: South Asia updates: Bangladesh skips BIMSTEC meet, Pakistan faces fresh turmoil - India Today

A day of fast-moving developments stretched from Dhaka and Islamabad to Kathmandu and London. The updates underscored rising regional strain, active crisis response and shifting political calculations.
A series of political, legal, economic and security developments unfolded across South Asia and beyond on Monday, with updates ranging from regional diplomacy and trade to court cases, accidents and disaster response.
Bangladesh said Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed will skip the first-ever meeting of home ministers of the BIMSTEC grouping in New Delhi, with a delegation led by a senior bureaucrat representing Dhaka amid strained ties with India. In Washington, a bipartisan group of US Senators questioned the legality of President Donald Trump's decision to allow diesel imports from Russia, saying it went against a law barring such trade until Moscow ends the war in Ukraine.
In Pakistan, two Army pilots were killed after their training aircraft crashed because of a technical fault, the army said. In another development, police took former Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and seven other leaders of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf into protective custody after emergency and governor's rule were imposed in the province.
A petition challenging the imposition of emergency and governor's rule in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province was filed in the Peshawar High Court on Monday, less than 24 hours after the measures were introduced.
In Sri Lanka, former president Mahinda Rajapaksa was admitted to hospital for urgent medical care and is under observation in the intensive care unit, his party said. Separately, a Sri Lankan court rejected an anticipatory bail plea filed by former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa, who had sought an order to prevent her arrest.
In the UK, the government said new deals worth 1 billion pounds had been unlocked as the first major British delegation arrived in India to maximise the benefits from the bilateral Free Trade Agreement.
In Nepal, Binod Chaudhary, the country's only billionaire, was elected vice president of the Nepali Congress, the main opposition party, along with Chandra Bhandari and Madhu Acharya at its 15th general convention in Kathmandu.
Nepalese authorities also continued search and rescue operations in Gorkha district, where five people remain missing after flash floods swept away homes and bridges. Authorities said 13 more people had been rescued from flood-affected areas.
In Bangladesh, the authorities stepped up security for Durga Puja amid concerns over minority safety. Officials put in place arrangements at nearly 33,000 venues across the country, including round-the-clock surveillance, specialised police units, and the use of drones and helicopters for idol immersion.
In Stockholm, American-born economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel memorial prize in economics for work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
Overall, the day's developments included Bangladesh's BIMSTEC decision and Durga Puja security measures, legal and political action in Pakistan and Sri Lanka, trade outreach by the UK in India, political and rescue updates from Nepal, questions in the US over Russian oil imports, and the Nobel economics prize announcement.

articles.title: India’s ₹34,284 crore Basmati trade gets a logistics boost with Iraq shipping plan - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: India’s ₹34,284 crore Basmati trade gets a logistics boost with Iraq shipping plan  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
IREF has introduced a bulk-shipping initiative aimed at cutting freight costs for Basmati rice exports to Iraq. This initiative will lower costs from $350 to $90 per tonne, significantly improving competitiveness in the Middle East market.
According to a press release issued by IREF on Monday, the initiative, undertaken in collaboration with Singapore-based Eximwala Solutions Pte. Ltd., covers bulk shipments of 1,02,210 metric tonnes of Basmati rice to Iraq through three vessels.
The initiative comes amid rising freight costs, container shortages and geopolitical disruptions affecting India's rice exports to the Middle East.
At these quoted rates, the reduction could translate into approximately $26.6 million in gross freight cost savings across the proposed three-vessel shipment volume.
The federation highlighted that the Middle East remains India's largest regional market for Basmati rice, accounting for nearly 70 per cent of the country's total Basmati export volume.
India exported 45.64 lakh metric tonnes of Basmati rice worth ₹34,284 crore to the Middle East during FY 2025-26. Including non-Basmati rice, India's total rice exports to the region stood at 56.48 lakh tonnes, valued at ₹39,657 crore.
Among major export destinations, Saudi Arabia imported Indian Basmati rice worth ₹8,324 crore, followed by Iran at ₹6,970 crore, Iraq at ₹5,583 crore and the UAE at ₹4,132 crore during the financial year.
Iraq alone imported approximately 7.64 lakh tonnes of Indian Basmati rice, underlining the importance of maintaining competitive shipping arrangements for Indian exporters.
IREF National Vice President Dev Garg said rising shipping costs directly affect India's competitiveness in the Middle East market, which accounts for a substantial share of the country's Basmati exports.
"The Middle East accounts for nearly 70 per cent of India's Basmati exports, and rising shipping costs directly affect our competitiveness. By targeting a reduction in freight from US$350 to US$90 per tonne, we are demonstrating how better logistics can benefit both Indian exporters and overseas buyers," Garg said.
He further added, "Our objective is to develop similar commercially viable solutions for other Gulf destinations, strengthen India's rice exports and improve returns across the value chain."
According to the federation, lower freight costs, improved shipping capacity and more reliable logistics could help Indian exporters offer competitive prices, protect their existing market share and expand trade with Iraq and other Gulf countries.
The initiative comes ahead of the Bharat International Rice Conference (BIRC) 2026, scheduled to take place from October 23 to 25 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi.
The conference will feature a dedicated session on shipping costs, bulk and container logistics, cargo insurance, port delays and maritime disputes, aimed at helping rice exporters reduce costs and protect profit margins.
IREF said the initiative is part of its broader vision of "One Nation, One Trade, One Policy", focused on reducing trade costs and strengthening India's position in global rice exports.

articles.summary: China says EU hybrid trade deal allows export growth from 2025 levels  CnEVPostEU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year  The GuardianLeapmotor-Stellantis JV calls EU-China import cap deal 'interesting alternative'  ET AutoChina holds intensive talks on hybrid, EV trade with EU  The Economic TimesChina, EU unveil fresh outcomes in auto trade talks; strong Chinese presence at Paris Motor Show 'underscores potential for deeper co-op' ...
articles.full_text:
- The commerce ministry said the arrangement allows growth from the 302,000 hybrid vehicles the EU imported from China in 2025.
- China said its quota would be no lower than that of any other source of EU imports, without disclosing specific volumes or an implementation timeline.
China's commerce ministry said its hybrid vehicle trade agreement with the European Union allows growth from 2025 import levels, ensuring room for Chinese companies to expand exports steadily.
In a statement responding to questions on Monday, the ministry elaborated on the principles underpinning the arrangement, after an EU statement that Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc would be halved drew attention.
The EU's hybrid vehicle imports from China rose to 302,000 in 2025 from 107,000 in 2024, the ministry said, citing Eurostat data.
The arrangement allows growth from the 2025 baseline and addresses the reasonable concerns of both sides' industries in light of market conditions, the ministry said. It did not disclose specific quotas, an implementation timeline or the extent of the increase.
The statement provides a new baseline for understanding the agreement, though information released by both sides remains insufficient to establish the scale of the final arrangement or how it will be implemented.
EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic said on October 9 that the agreement included halving China's exports of hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) to the bloc.
He did not specify the baseline for that reduction. China's latest statement also did not explain how his remarks relate to an arrangement allowing growth from 2025 levels.
The ministry said the 2 sides had confirmed 3 basic principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with rules. Any measures would neither specifically target Chinese products nor discriminate against Chinese companies.
China's quota would be no lower than that of any other source of EU imports, the ministry said, adding that both sides had affirmed the trade arrangement should comply with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
China also reserves all rights under the WTO framework, including recourse to dispute settlement and requests for trade compensation, the ministry said. The principles are intended to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies.
The clarification followed talks between Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and Sefcovic in Beijing on October 8 and 9, after which both sides announced an understanding on hybrid vehicle trade.
Hybrids have become a new focus of China-EU automotive trade talks. The EU imposed definitive countervailing duties on China-made battery electric vehicles (BEVs) in October 2024, while hybrids were excluded from those measures.
Bloomberg reported on October 7, citing people familiar with the matter, that the EU was preparing safeguard measures for hybrid vehicles that could restrict imports through tariff-rate quotas.
On BEVs, the ministry said the 2 sides achieved a "soft landing" in the anti-subsidy case in January this year, when the EU issued general guidance on price undertakings.

Bangladesh NCP Leader Nahid Islam Backs CJP Protests Amid India Row
Bangladesh NCP convenor Nahid Islam backs CJP-led protests in India, drawing attention to political tensions, minority safety and reported anti-India remarks.
Bangladesh’s National Citizen Party (NCP) convenor Nahid Islam has backed protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in India, raising fresh political questions amid tensions between the two countries. His statement focused on electoral accountability and the safety of minorities. However, reported remarks by another NCP leader about India’s Northeast have added to the controversy surrounding the party.
What Did Nahid Islam Say?
Nahid Islam issued a statement from Dhaka expressing support for protesters in India who were raising concerns about electoral accountability. He also argued that a society cannot be considered truly democratic if its minority communities live in fear.
His remarks have drawn attention because of the wider political situation in Bangladesh and the concerns raised in India over statements made by some Bangladeshi political leaders.
The statement has also brought the NCP into the spotlight at a time when relations between India and Bangladesh remain an important regional issue.
Why Is the NCP Facing Questions?
The National Citizen Party emerged from the political unrest that led to the removal of Sheikh Hasina's government in August 2024. Several NCP leaders played prominent roles in the movement during that period.
The party has also been reported to have formed an alliance with Jamaat-e-Islami, a political group with an Islamist background. This association has attracted attention in discussions about Bangladesh's changing political landscape.
Criticism of the NCP has also focused on statements attributed to some of its leaders about India. These remarks have added another dimension to the debate over the party's political position and its approach towards its neighbouring country.
What Is the Seven Sisters Controversy?
India's Seven Sisters are the northeastern states of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. The region is strategically important because of its location and its links with the rest of India through the narrow Siliguri Corridor.
In December 2025, Youth Tipra Federation president Suraj Debbarma raised concerns over alleged anti-India statements by Bangladeshi leaders. He referred to claims attributed to NCP leader Hasnat Abdullah about capturing the Seven Sisters and the Siliguri Corridor.
These reported remarks triggered concerns about regional security and relations between the two countries. However, such statements should be understood as allegations attributed to political figures, rather than evidence of an official government policy.
Dipu Chandra Das Case Raises Minority Safety Concerns
The question of minority safety in Bangladesh has also remained a major point of discussion. The reference material describes the killing of Dipu Chandra Das, a 27-year-old Hindu garment factory worker, in Mymensingh in December 2025.
According to the account, he was accused of blasphemy before a mob attacked and killed him. His body was reportedly tied to a tree and set on fire.
The case drew attention to the dangers of mob violence and the need to protect people from attacks based on allegations or religious differences. It also forms part of the wider debate about the safety of Bangladesh's Hindu community.
Nahid Islam's comments about minority protection have therefore attracted scrutiny, given the concerns surrounding reported attacks on minorities in Bangladesh.
What Does This Mean for India-Bangladesh Relations?
Political statements from either country can affect public opinion and add pressure to already sensitive diplomatic relations. India and Bangladesh share important economic, cultural and security interests, making stable relations valuable to both sides.
The reported comments about India's Northeast have raised concerns because the region holds strategic importance. At the same time, political disagreements and protests require careful handling to avoid increasing tensions between ordinary citizens.
Nahid Islam's support for the CJP-led protests has added a new talking point to the debate. The key questions now concern the statements made by political leaders, the protection of minorities and the future direction of relations between the neighbouring countries.

articles.title: GE Aerospace to nearly double supplier spend in India by 2030, eyes growing aviation demand - The Economic Times
articles.summary: GE Aerospace to nearly double supplier spend in India by 2030, eyes growing aviation demand  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
GE Aerospace has announced plans to nearly double its spending on Indian suppliers between 2025 and 2030, as the company looks to strengthen its domestic supply chain and support India's rapidly expanding aviation sector.
The announcement was made alongside the release of a report by Ernst & Young (EY), titled 'Powering Progress: GE Aerospace's Economic Impact in India', which assesses the company's economic contribution to India's commercial aviation, defence, manufacturing and engineering sectors over four decades.
The report was released at India Taking Flight - Aviation, Innovation and the Road to Viksit Bharat 2047, an event hosted by GE Aerospace and attended by industry leaders.
According to the report, GE Aerospace spent approximately $200 million on its Indian supply chain in 2025. The company plans to double this expenditure by 2030 to meet rising demand and expand its network of domestic suppliers, including small and medium-sized enterprises.
India's commercial aviation sector continues to witness significant growth, with domestic airlines generating approximately $19 billion in revenue in the financial year 2025-26 (FY26). GE Aerospace's advanced engine technology and operational reliability contribute to the efficiency and connectivity of India's aviation ecosystem, which supports an estimated 370,000 direct jobs.
As of December 2025, commercial engines manufactured by GE Aerospace and its partners powered the majority of commercial airline operations in India, with a fleet of more than 1,400 engines. The report states that these engines have helped Indian carriers achieve a passenger load factor of 88.2%, the highest globally, while aircraft utilisation rates have reached 12 to 14 hours per day, significantly exceeding global figures.
Commenting on the announcement, Vikram Rai, CEO, South Asia, GE Aerospace, said India's commercial aviation growth was among the fastest in the world and highlighted the company's contribution beyond engine sales.
He said the company's presence in India extends from component manufacturing in Pune to engineering and innovation in Bengaluru, while its partnerships with Indian customers and suppliers are helping build the next generation of the country's aerospace industry.Rai added that increasing supplier spending would strengthen the domestic supply chain and help meet growing demand as India works towards its Viksit Bharat ambitions.
The report highlights the significant growth expected in India's aviation industry over the coming decades. According to Government of India estimates cited in the report, annual domestic passenger traffic is projected to reach 1.1 billion by 2040, compared with 340 million in FY26.
The country's airport network is also expected to expand from 163 airports to more than 350 by 2047, creating greater demand for aircraft, engines, maintenance services and aviation infrastructure.
To meet the projected demand, India and South Asia will require approximately 3,300 additional aircraft, equivalent to 6,600 additional engines, by 2044.
In July 2026, IndiGo announced a memorandum of understanding with CFM International for an order of more than 1,000 LEAP-1A engines to power 510 Airbus A320neo Family aircraft. The agreement represents the largest single order ever placed for LEAP engines and a record for CFM International. It also includes support for establishing IndiGo's upcoming engine maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) facility.
GE Aerospace and its partner engines are expected to power most of the approximately 1,500 new aircraft already on order with Indian carriers. The report estimates that this presents an opportunity worth more than $5.5 billion for India's MRO industry, potentially strengthening the country's position as a regional hub for aircraft engine maintenance and repair.
GE Aerospace's manufacturing operations in India are centred around its flagship facility in Pune, which was established with an initial investment of $200 million. Since 2024, the company has invested nearly $55 million in expanding automation, improving precision-manufacturing capabilities and advancing workforce development at the facility.
These investments have strengthened its manufacturing capabilities and supported a wider domestic supply chain comprising 17 major Indian partners, including small and medium-sized enterprises.
The company's plan to nearly double supplier spending by 2030 is expected to further expand opportunities for Indian manufacturers and suppliers as demand for aircraft engines and related components increases. Workforce development remains another key area of focus. Since 2015, approximately 5,000 production associates have graduated from the Pune facility's apprenticeship programme, which enrols between 400 and 500 new apprentices every year.
The programme aims to develop manufacturing skills and build a workforce capable of supporting the growing requirements of the aerospace industry.GE Aerospace also highlighted its long-standing partnership with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), which began in 1986 and remains an important part of India's efforts to strengthen domestic defence manufacturing.
The partnership covers LM2500 naval engines and F404-IN20 engines that power India's Tejas Mk1 light combat aircraft. According to the company, the F404 platform has more than 4,000 engines deployed across 16 countries.
In 2023, GE Aerospace signed a memorandum of understanding covering the potential domestic manufacture of F414 engines for the Tejas Mk2 programme. However, the proposed manufacturing arrangement remains subject to final agreements and necessary approvals.
The company has also signed a five-year Performance Based Logistics contract with the Indian Air Force for Apache helicopter engines. In a separate agreement, it has committed to establishing an in-country depot facility for F404-IN20 engines.
These initiatives are aimed at strengthening domestic maintenance and support capabilities, improving the availability of defence platforms and contributing to India's broader defence self-reliance objectives.
GE Aerospace's Bengaluru Technology Centre, established in 2000 with an investment of $200 million, has emerged as a key centre for research, engineering and technological innovation.
The facility was among the first research and engineering centres of its kind established outside the United States. Since its inception, it has secured more than 1,000 aviation patents and contributed to the design, development and certification of the GE9X engine, described by the company as the world's most powerful jet engine.
Engineers at the Bengaluru centre hold key design responsibilities for the GE90, GP7200, GEnx and GE9X engines. They are also playing a significant role in the CFM RISE programme, which aims to improve fuel efficiency by 20% while meeting customer expectations for durability.
The centre's Digital Technology team also supports GE Aerospace's global supply chain, MRO and sales operations through the application of artificial intelligence.
In addition to its engineering work, the company is investing in the development of India's aerospace talent through academic partnerships and research programmes. These include a flagship joint innovation programme with IIT Madras, which has produced a locally designed and manufactured Micro Turbomachine.
The initiative reflects the growing role of Indian engineering institutions and research centres in developing technologies for the global aerospace industry.
The EY report brings together GE Aerospace's contributions across manufacturing, engineering, commercial aviation and defence over the past four decades.
The company's investments in Pune and Bengaluru, its partnerships with Indian suppliers and HAL, and its workforce development initiatives form part of its strategy to expand its presence in the country.
With India's aviation sector expected to grow substantially over the next two decades, the planned increase in domestic supplier spending is intended to strengthen the local manufacturing ecosystem, expand engineering capabilities and support the rising demand for aircraft engines and maintenance services.
The announcement comes as India seeks to expand its aviation infrastructure, strengthen domestic manufacturing and advance its Viksit Bharat 2047 vision. GE Aerospace's proposed increase in supplier spending is expected to create further opportunities for Indian manufacturers and engineering talent while reinforcing the country's role in the global aerospace supply chain.
Synopsis
The announcement was made alongside the release of a report by Ernst & Young (EY), titled 'Powering Progress: GE Aerospace's Economic Impact in India', which assesses the company's economic contribution to India's commercial aviation, defence, manufacturing and engineering sectors over four decades.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal stated that India is poised to become a global car manufacturing hub as growing demand makes local production viable. He noted that trade deals protect the mass-market vehicle segment while luxury carmakers expand operations.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has expressed confidence that India could emerge as a global car manufacturing hub as demand grows enough to make local production commercially viable for international automakers.
Speaking at the ‘Dilli Dialogue: Policies for a Future-Ready India’ in New Delhi, Goyal said the import quotas permitted under India’s trade agreements with the United Kingdom and the European Union largely cover expensive cars, while the mass-market segment for vehicles priced below ₹17 lakh remains protected.
He cited luxury carmakers setting up manufacturing plants in Pune after initially testing the Indian market as an example of how international manufacturers could expand production in India as demand grows.
Goyal also said European Union regulations could make car manufacturing in the bloc less competitive and encourage companies to shift more production to India.
“Tatas had so much trouble after they bought Jaguar. Tata Motors itself was going to collapse and then they put in a lot of re-engineering, and shift some models to India. Finally they were able to make money after years,” he said.
Electronics, tourism and jobs
Goyal said India needed a two-pronged approach: adopting the world's best technologies while identifying sectors with significant potential to create jobs and businesses.
He pointed to rising demand for electronics and white goods as an opportunity to attract investment into domestic manufacturing, including semiconductor fabrication plants.
Tourism, he said, was another sector with considerable potential to generate employment and create new business opportunities. Artificial intelligence could make tourism promotion more efficient, but human experiences would remain central to the industry.
“AI can only add to the efficiency of promoting tourism. But otherwise, human experiences will always be AI proof,” he said.
India’s workforce and trade strategy
Highlighting India's demographic advantage, Goyal referred to demand for Indian workers in countries such as Germany and Japan. He said people from the North-East could serve as India's brand ambassadors in nursing and caregiving, while describing the region as a gateway to ASEAN and the Far East.
Goyal said he had participated in 10 bilateral meetings with foreign counterparts on the sidelines of the G20 meeting in the US last month. He added that he was scheduled to meet ministers from the UK and Canada in New Delhi on October 12 and 13, respectively.
He also criticised trade decisions taken by the previous United Progressive Alliance (UPA) government, referring to a Cabinet resolution on Vietnam's market-economy status and free trade agreements involving the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) and ASEAN.
Goyal said India had trade agreements with Australia, New Zealand, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and the European Union that excluded dairy products to protect the interests of small farmers.
He added that he did not believe other trade ministers viewed politeness as a sign of weakness.

The IMF has raised India's GDP growth forecast by 60 basis points to 7% for FY27, citing resilient domestic demand and robust services activity. - India's economy is projected to grow at 7% in FY27, driven by strong domestic demand and services.
- The country stands out with upward revisions amidst a weakening global medium-term outlook.

A basis point equals one-hundredth of a percentage point, commonly used in finance to express precise changes in interest rates, yields, or economic projections. Revisions stated in basis points avoid ambiguity when changes are small but financially significant.
A forward-looking estimate of the rate at which the CPI — a weighted basket of consumer goods and services — is expected to rise over a defined period. Central banks and multilateral institutions use CPI inflation forecasts to calibrate monetary policy and assess purchasing power erosion.

After RBI, World Bank, IMF raise India’s GDP growth forecast, expect economy to grow at 7% in FY27
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised its growth forecast for the Indian economy to 7% for FY27, following similar upgrades by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the World Bank last week. The IMF has revised its projection upwards by 60 basis points, citing resilient domestic demand and robust services activity.
The IMF has also raised its GDP growth estimate for FY28 by 30 basis points to 7%, according to its latest World Economic Outlook released on Tuesday.
“India remains among the fastest-growing major economies, with growth in 2026 projected at 7.0%,” the IMF said in its report, attributing the outlook to “stronger-than-expected momentum, supported by resilient domestic demand and robust services activity”.
On a calendar-year basis, the IMF expects India’s economy to grow by 7.4% in 2026 and 7% in 2027. The RBI and the World Bank have both raised their growth forecasts for India in FY27 to 7.1%, according to their latest projections.
On the inflation front, the IMF expects India’s consumer price index (CPI) inflation to average 5% in FY27 before easing to 4.4% in FY28. Its forecast for the current financial year is lower than the RBI’s latest estimate of 5.2%.
India stands out in medium-term outlook
The IMF expects India’s growth momentum to remain strong over the medium term, supported by favourable demographic dynamics, a large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms.
“India stands out with upward revisions, reflecting sustained momentum and growing evidence of stronger growth potential supported by favorable demographic dynamics, a large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms,” the report said.
While the medium-term outlook has weakened for several economies since January 2026, India has received upward revisions. Downgrades are concentrated among economies directly affected by the conflict in the Middle East and energy-importing emerging and developing economies elsewhere, excluding India.
The IMF projects global output to expand at an average annual pace of 3.2% between 2028 and 2031, below the pre-pandemic average of 3.7% recorded during 2000–2019.
The report said countries’ ability to adapt to geopolitical and technological changes would determine their medium-term growth potential. “Readiness to adopt AI and to reliably meet energy needs will be crucial,” it said, adding that countries more dependent on fossil fuels for power generation are more exposed to geopolitical shocks.
Global growth outlook remains uneven
The IMF has raised its global growth forecast for 2026 by 10 basis points to 3.1%, while retaining its projection for 2027 at 3.4%.
Advanced economies are projected to grow by 2.1% in 2026, compared with 2% in 2025. Growth in emerging market and developing economies is expected to slow to 3.7% in 2026 from 4.5% in 2025, before recovering to 4.4% in 2027, as per the report.
Within Asia, China’s growth is projected to slow to 4.5% in 2026 as higher global oil prices, persistent uncertainty and structural headwinds weigh on economic activity. Policy support is expected to prevent a sharper slowdown.
As per the report, global economic activity held up better than expected in the first half of 2026, although growth varied across countries. India continued to record robust growth, underpinned by domestic demand and services despite higher oil prices. China’s second-quarter growth, meanwhile, came in at 4.3% year-on-year.
The IMF, however, warned that “a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East or Ukraine could make commodity prices higher and more volatile for longer”, exacerbating inflationary pressures. Further disruptions to major energy transit routes and supply chains remain key risks to the global outlook.

articles.full_text:
By Eleonora Mavroeidi, Abhishek Gupta and Maeva Cousin
A more protectionist US could prove an unexpected tailwind for India’s economy. As countries redraw supply chains around trusted partners and seek preferential market access, New Delhi has ended years of caution and is rapidly expanding its free-trade network.
Using a large-scale model of the global economy developed by the World Trade Organization, we estimate these agreements could add about $140 billion to India’s GDP in 2035, opening new markets, cutting import costs, fostering foreign direct investment and lifting productivity. 
We also consider two scenarios that could amplify the gains: realizing further productivity benefits from a decade of reforms to strengthen manufacturing competitiveness, and enacting policies that help underemployed agricultural workers transition into manufacturing and services.
The Great Redrawing of Global Trade Maps
The surge in US tariffs since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 is redrawing global trade links. After 19 months of wild swings, we estimate the average US tariff rate stood at 10.7% in August, up from 2.3% in 2024. That reflects sectoral tariffs—mainly on cars and metals, and country-specific levies set at around 10%-12.5% under the Section 301 forced labor action. Tariffs at this rate could lower US goods imports by roughly 15% compared with the previous regime. Threats and investigations point to more hikes to come.
Other countries are responding by diversifying trade links and accelerating negotiations with new partners. Since the start of 2025, the European Union has signed new or updated agreements with Mercosur and Mexico and concluded negotiations with Indonesia, India and Australia. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations and China signed an upgraded free-trade agreement in October 2025. Canada signed several agreements in 2025-26 and moved to launch, accelerate or revive others.
 
India is no exception. During 2025-26, agreements with the European Free Trade Association, the UK and Oman entered into force, adding to deals with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022. India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded negotiations with the EU. In addition, New Delhi is pursuing other partners—including the Eurasian Economic Union—and has sought an agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council.
At the same time, India has pursued deeper trade links with the US since Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced plans for a bilateral agreement in February 2025. The relationship has been rocky. In the second half of 2025, India faced some of the highest additional tariffs among major US trading partners after Washington imposed a 25% reciprocal tariff and an additional 25% duty linked to Russian oil purchases.
 
Tensions have eased since then. While sectoral tariffs remain in place, the US removed the Russia-related 25% tariff and lowered reciprocal rates on India to 18% in February. In addition, under the Section 301 forced labor action, which has replaced reciprocal tariffs, India has been set a rate of 10%, lower than the 12.5% slapped on many other partners. This is paving the way for an interim deal, though reaching a more comprehensive agreement may prove difficult.
What Trade Reshuffling Means for the Indian Economy
Using a computable general equilibrium model, we estimate how India’s trade deals could reshape its economy over the next decade.
 
We start by assessing the impact of US tariffs at their August level, relative to 2024 duties. We calculate that the average tariff on Indian goods sold to the US has risen to 11.6%, from 2.4% in 2024. By 2035, we estimate the tariffs will cut Indian goods exports to the US by about one-fifth. But the hit to India’s economy should be limited. Less than 2% of its output relies on US markets, and stronger exports elsewhere should cushion the blow. We estimate the effect on gross domestic product will be negligible.
We then model the FTAs already concluded or under negotiation through three channels:
 
- First, we adjust bilateral tariffs using a stylized schedule that captures the key elements of the deals. India’s partners eliminate all tariffs on Indian goods in the first year. India eliminates tariffs on industrial products and halves those on agricultural products, implementing half of the reduction in the first year and the rest by year 10.
- Second, building on Metivier et al. (2023), we assume the cost of nontariff measures on goods and services falls gradually by 25% over 15 years, with an additional reduction in NTMs on services to capture lower uncertainty from bilateral agreements.
- Third, using Prasad et al. (2008), we add a productivity boost from higher FDI in line with commitments under the deals: $100 billion over 15 years for EFTA (roughly $35 billion of which is expected to be additional), and $20 billion for New Zealand (almost all additional). 
For US-India negotiations, we model an interim agreement under which India grants the US roughly the same tariff reductions as under its other deals. The US cuts sectoral duties on automotive products to 15% (including most-favored-nation tariffs) but keeps the 50% metal tariffs and 10% Section 301 duties on most covered products—similar to the conditions it granted other deal partners such as the EU or Japan. We still expect the agreement to reduce tensions and uncertainty and to deliver the same decline in NTMs as India’s other FTAs.
 
Our analysis suggests FTAs already in force should raise India’s GDP by 1.2% by 2035 relative to baseline, rising to 1.7% if the EU and New Zealand agreements are implemented from 2027, a gain of about $140 billion at constant 2025 US dollars. A US deal would add 0.2 percentage point. If negotiations with the EAEU, GCC and Israel conclude over the next few years, the gain could rise by another 0.2 ppt, leaving GDP 2.1% higher (about $170 billion) by 2035.
Trade volumes would rise even faster. By 2035, Indian exports could be almost 10% above baseline if all deals are implemented. Imports also would climb as households and businesses gain access to new products and services and manufacturers become more integrated into global value chains.
How Domestic Trends Could Compound the Boost
Signing FTAs is only the first step. Reaping the full benefits will require India to sustain its reform momentum. Effective implementation; reliable access to energy, critical minerals and advanced technologies; and unlocking the potential of India’s vast labor force will all be important.
We model an upside scenario in which two domestic trends amplify the gains:
- Lower production costs. India has cut corporate taxes, introduced subsidies, ramped up infrastructure investment to lower logistics costs and funded incentives to boost workers’ skills. Regardless of trade developments, some of these benefits likely have already materialized. In this upside scenario we assume a further boost to manufacturers’ efficiency, which we model as a roughly 2% decline in production costs. That could add roughly 1 ppt to export gains and 0.5 ppt to GDP gains by 2035.
- Tap India’s agricultural labor potential. More than 40% of Indian workers remain in agriculture—little changed over the past decade—with high underemployment. By comparison, in rapidly industrializing Vietnam the share has fallen from more than 40% to around 25%, while agricultural output per worker has risen rapidly and now exceeds India’s by almost 60%. We model a similar productivity boost in India phased in over a decade, allowing workers to shift toward expanding manufacturing and services. This adds slightly more than 1 ppt to export growth and about 2 ppts to GDP gains. 
India is pairing an ambitious industrial strategy with an equally ambitious trade agenda. If it gets the combination right, it could become a powerful new engine of long-term growth. US tariffs are a drag. For India, and the world, the right response could yet deliver a development win.

Could Asim Munir repeat Egypt’s historic...  Moneycontrol.comFrom Brotherly Neighbour to Saudi Proxy. Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
When Pakistan was trying to plug a $3bn financial hole in April, Saudi Arabia swung to the rescue with an emergency bailout that underscored Islamabad’s deep reliance on the House of Saud.
Now, as missiles from Iran-backed Houthi militants rain down on Saudi cities and Saudi-backed forces mount a renewed offensive in Yemen, Riyadh has activated a mutual defence pact, drawing Pakistan into a conflict it spent months trying to avoid — and one that is deeply unpopular at home.
After a missile strike on Saturday killed 13 people and injured hundreds at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reaffirmed Islamabad’s “steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security”. A separate strike on the facility on Sunday killed a Pakistani national.
Pakistan has long sent troops and military trainers to Saudi Arabia. Islamabad delivered a squadron of fighter jets and pilots to protect Saudi Arabia from Iranian missiles and drones after the April bailout was agreed.
But Islamabad had hoped that its diplomatic capital — built up by mediating a ceasefire between Iran and the US — and deterrence would help it avoid direct involvement in renewed fighting in Yemen.
“Now that the Yemen front has gotten hot, Pakistan is faced with balancing two opposing choices,” said Ejaz Haider, a Lahore-based foreign policy writer. He pointed to Islamabad’s “financial dependence on the Saudi state and remittances from workers” on the one hand, and its desire to “[limit] being dragged into this slug fest in Yemen” on the other.
In recent months, Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s de facto leader, has leaned on Iran’s leaders to rein in the Houthis and Shia militias in Iraq that have targeted Saudi Arabia.
In August, Pakistan renewed its security commitments to Saudi Arabia with the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which drew in Turkey, following the signing of a bilateral pact between Islamabad and Riyadh last year.
“Pakistan’s attempts to diplomatically resolve or at least freeze the situation by asking Iran to restrain the Houthis have failed,” said Umer Karim, a researcher on Pakistan-Saudi relations at the University of Birmingham. “Pakistan and Iran are now arrayed against each other in Yemen.”
Last week, the signatories of the Mecca pact announced that Islamabad and Ankara would “provide the agreed military forces and capabilities” to Saudi Arabia after the Houthis resumed targeting Saudi oil installations and tankers and made extensive territorial gains along the Red Sea coast, seizing control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a critical maritime trade route.
Pakistan’s military has vowed that it would “go to any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
Pakistan has considerable military resources to bear. Its armed forces field more than 660,000 soldiers and 400 fighter and ground-attack aircraft, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, including Chinese-Pakistani JF-17s and US-made F-16s. It also produces drones for combat and surveillance, some in collaboration with Turkey.
Islamabad’s forces have been hardened by two decades of counter-insurgency along its restive western frontier as well as skirmishes with arch-enemy India, including a conflict last year in which it claimed to have shot down six of New Delhi’s fighter jets.
But the military’s record on curbing militancy is weak. Insurgents killed more than 1,200 Pakistani security forces last year, the highest death toll in more than 20 years, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal, a New Delhi-based platform. Violence along the border with Taliban-ruled Afghanistan has also worsened, despite air strikes in recent months.
It is not yet clear the extent of Pakistan’s involvement. A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said last week that 100 fighter jets took part in an air campaign against the Houthis. Neither Islamabad nor Ankara has confirmed if their nations’ pilots participated. The Pakistan Armed Forces said it could not confirm or deny any operational details.
One person in Islamabad briefed on the matter said Pakistan had “provided support” to “the joint operation” but did not specify what equipment or personnel were involved.
But public opposition to outright military involvement in Yemen is widespread.
Much of Pakistan, which includes a large Shia minority, supports the Iranian regime that it sees as standing up to the US and Israel. Thousands mourned when Iran’s former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in late February.
“The people of Pakistan have little appetite to fight a war on behalf of the House of Saud, which would in effect put them on the side of the US and against Iran,” said Haider.
Islamabad has resisted Saudi calls to arms before. In 2015, when Riyadh asked for warships, planes and ground troops in Yemen, Pakistan, led by popular prime minister Nawaz Sharif, demurred. Parliament unanimously passed resolution to “maintain neutrality”.
This time, analysts said, there would be no such public debate. The current government of Shehbaz Sharif, Nawaz’s brother, has a weak base of support and relies on military backing.
The full details of both defence pacts with Saudi Arabia have yet to be made public, and neither document has been presented to parliament for approval.
Pakistan’s options are also constrained by its fragile finances.
Alongside the $3bn emergency loan, Riyadh issued a three-year extension on a $5bn deposit with Islamabad’s central bank — together equivalent to about 38 per cent of its reserves. Migrant labourers in the Gulf kingdom sent home $9.78bn in remittances last year.
Ultimately, said Karim: “Pakistan is in a bind as its commitments towards Saudi Arabia are increasingly pulling it into the war in Yemen which can damage its mediation role [with Iran] and create a degree of additional domestic discontent.”
