articles.title: The Waiver Is the Policy: What 19 October Will Reveal About Who Washington Really Sanctions - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: The Waiver Is the Policy: What 19 October Will Reveal About Who Washington Really Sanctions  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
A Licence Signed Before the Ink Was Dry
On 9 October, three weeks after Donald Trump signed the most sweeping Russia sanctions statute of his presidency, the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (the agency that writes and enforces US sanctions) issued General License 135. The licence allows Russian-origin diesel to be sold, shipped and imported into the United States until 7 April 2027.
Most coverage treated the licence as a contradiction of the new law. It is the law working as designed. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act gives the president a national-interest waiver over almost every mandatory measure it contains, and the diesel licence is the first public sign of how that waiver will be used. When the Act’s 30-day deadline arrives on 19 October, the question will not be how hard Washington hits Russia. It will be who gets spared, and why.
Mandatory on Paper, Optional in Practice
The Act, signed on 18 September, does three things that matter for business. First, it requires blocking sanctions on Sberbank, VTB, Gazprombank and other state-owned Russian banks, and it exposes foreign banks that do “significant transactions” with them to secondary sanctions. Second, it orders designations of vessels carrying Russian energy, along with their owners, insurers and the ports that service them. Third, under Section 113, it authorises tariffs of up to 100% on all goods from countries that are among the five largest importers of Russian crude or gas and keep buying after the deadline, or that are among the top five hubs for sanctions evasion.
The statute names no countries. Senate aides’ indicative crude list is China, India, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan, and some assessments add Turkey. Every one of these measures can be switched off under Section 115 with a written certification to Congress that doing so serves the national interest. That is a reporting requirement, not a veto.
Sanctions That Cost American Voters Nothing
The useful way to read 19 October is as a cost sort. Washington will enforce the Act where the price falls on Russia, and waive it where the price would fall on American fuel buyers. US diesel averaged $6.51 a gallon last week, nearly double a year ago, and retail diesel is up about 70% since the Iran war began. Farm-state Senate seats that Republicans assumed were safe are now competitive. Iowa’s open seat polls as a toss-up, and Republicans are pouring late money into Kansas and Nebraska. Diesel is what moves combines and lorries, and three weeks before the 3 November midterms, it is the variable the White House is optimising.
Apply that filter and the map draws itself.
Most likely to be hit: Russian state banks and the shadow fleet. Sanctioning Sberbank and VTB costs American consumers nothing, because they have been largely cut off from the US financial system since 2022. Vessel designations are similarly cheap and highly visible. Expect a substantial list on or near the deadline, because the administration needs something to show the bipartisan coalition that is already attacking the diesel deal. The fine print matters, though. In August, 61% of Russian crude moved on already-sanctioned shadow tankers, but 72% of Russian oil products moved on Western-owned or Western-insured ships. Designations aimed at crude carriers hurt Moscow. Designations aimed at product tankers would undo GL 135, so they are unlikely.
Most likely to be spared: China and the diesel trade. China has taken about half of Russia’s crude exports since late 2022 and is the most obvious Section 113 target. It is also the country Washington just extended a trade truce with, running to January, after Xi’s first state visit in 11 years. A 100% tariff on $308.7bn of annual imports weeks before an election would be inflationary self-harm. Expect a waiver framed as “ongoing negotiations”.
The real test: India. India is where the cost sort gets hard, and where this argument departs from the consensus. Most analysts see India as the obvious target: Russian crude reached a record 50.8% of its imports in July, despite New Delhi’s February pledge to halt Russian purchases in exchange for a tariff cut to 18%. But India is also a diesel refinery for the West. Indian, Turkish and other refineries running Russian crude shipped €510m of oil products to sanctioning countries in August, €143m of it to the United States. Penalising India’s crude purchases now would cut diesel supply to the very market the White House is trying to calm. So the Section 113 tariff will be used as leverage over a trade deal Indian officials call “99 percent” done, not as a penalty.
The European edge cases. Hungary and Slovakia still take Russian crude through the Druzhba pipeline, and the Act’s carve-out covers only gas. Budapest’s new government is lobbying Congress for relief before Orbán’s old one-year exemption expires on 21 November. European firms face a mirror-image problem. Brussels is tightening its own regime, which MD has tracked in Europe’s record Russia blacklist, while Washington licenses the trade Europe bans. A shipper can now be compliant in New York and in breach in Rotterdam on the same voyage.
The strongest objection is that Congress wrote the law precisely to tie the president’s hands, with a veto-proof bipartisan majority behind it. If the White House waives too much, the argument goes, Congress will force enforcement. That is true in principle and weak in timing. Section 115 waivers require a certification and a report, not congressional consent. Members are campaigning until November. And the waiver only needs to hold for three weeks. Daniel Fried, a former US sanctions coordinator, put the risk plainly before the Act passed: the danger was never abuse but waivers and little use of the tough provisions. The diesel licence suggests he was right. The real enforcement decision has been deferred to after 3 November and the first 180-day review, when the trade-off shifts.
Three Ways 19 October Can Go
Base case: hard on Moscow, soft on markets (about 60%). Treasury designates the Russian state banks, sanctions a large batch of crude-carrying shadow tankers, and touts it as the biggest Russia action of the year. No Section 113 tariff takes effect. China is waived under the truce, and India and Hungary receive “negotiation” notices instead of duties. GL 135 stays in place. This rests on one assumption: diesel stays above $6 through polling day. For compliance teams, the risk falls on shipowners and insurers of crude cargoes, not on importers in buyer countries.
Downside case: India pays for the diesel deal (about 25%). Stung by the bipartisan backlash and by Trump’s own call for Ukraine to replace Zelensky, which turned the diesel licence into a political liability, the White House sends Congress the required 10-day notice and names India at a token rate, perhaps 10–25%, to show it is serious. The trigger would be the Fitzpatrick bill gaining Republican co-sponsors. Indian exporters of pharmaceuticals, textiles and auto parts would face duties stacked on top of existing tariffs, and Indian refiners would cut Russian intake, tightening global diesel just as winter demand peaks. Few readers are pricing this in, because it looks irrational. It becomes rational only if the White House calculates that seeming soft on Russia now costs more votes than diesel does.
Alternative case: Congress takes the pen (about 15%). Republican senators in exposed farm states break publicly with the diesel deal. Treasury narrows GL 135 to volumes already contracted and lets it lapse early, and the first 180-day review becomes a genuine enforcement event. This would turn the Act from a menu back into a mandate, the outcome its authors intended, but it needs Congress to act against the president’s fuel policy in an election season.
Probabilities reflect the author’s analytical judgment based on currently available information and are not statistical forecasts.
Read the Notices, Not the Statute
The Graham Act will be remembered less for what it mandated than for what it allowed the president to waive. On 19 October, Washington will sanction where sanctions are cheap, in Russian banks and crude tankers, and waive where they are expensive, in diesel, Chinese trade and the Indian refineries that turn Russian crude into fuel for American farms. Moscow’s behaviour barely enters the calculation.
The signal to watch is procedural. Section 113 requires a written justification to Congress at least 10 days before any tariff is imposed. If no such notice has been filed, no secondary tariff can lawfully land on the deadline, whatever the headlines say. The first Section 115 certifications filed the same week will tell you who was spared by name.
Congress wrote a sanctions law about Russia. The White House is enforcing a fuel policy about Iowa.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended the Trump administration’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major convicted of killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in Texas, dismissing concerns that the broadcast could fuel radicalisation or turn him into a martyr.
“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said in an interview with CBS News’ 
Face the Nation
 on Sunday.
“If you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime,” he added.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3 for the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, in which 13 people were killed and 32 others injured.
The plan to broadcast his execution live, announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has drawn criticism from both Republicans and Democrats. President Donald Trump has backed the idea but has not made a final decision on whether the execution will be televised.
Mullin said the administration had considered the potential risks and argued that viewers would not be forced to watch the broadcast.
“No one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” he told CBS News.
However, critics have warned that broadcasting the execution could give extremist groups propaganda material and increase security risks for Americans at home and abroad.
Alaska Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski called the proposal “gruesome”, arguing that it could give Hasan the martyrdom he sought.
“It's something I would expect from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America,” she wrote on X, adding that the way the US carries out justice matters as much as the justice itself.
Virginia Democratic Senator Mark Warner also cautioned that a public execution could provide terrorist organisations with a propaganda victory, fuel radicalisation and put American service members, diplomats and citizens overseas at greater risk.
Hasan, who was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair, admitted to killing the unarmed troops at a crowded medical facility at Fort Hood. During his trial, he said he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.
If carried out, Hasan’s execution would be the first by the US military since 1961 and its first firing-squad execution since World War II. A public broadcast would also mark the first public execution in the United States in nearly a century.

Bangladesh is heading for its weakest economic growth in nearly four decades in the current 2026-27 fiscal year, with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projecting GDP growth of just 3.2%, lower than forecasts from both the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.
The forecast is further clouded by the lender's projection that inflation will surge to 10.9%, according to its World Economic Outlook published today (13 October), pointing to another difficult year for an economy struggling to regain momentum.
The last time growth was this weak was in FY1988-89, when GDP expanded by 3.11%, according to Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) data. Even during the Covid-19 pandemic, the economy grew 3.45% in FY2019-20.
The IMF's growth forecast for Bangladesh is also lower than those of other international lenders. The World Bank has projected growth of 3.4% for FY2026-27, while the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has forecast 4%.
Against this backdrop, Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury appealed to development partners, particularly the IMF and the World Bank, for support at the IMF-World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok. Today, he met IMF Executive Director Urjit Patel and World Bank Managing Director of Operations Anna Bjerde.
In its April forecast, the IMF projected Bangladesh's growth at 4.3% for FY2026-27. The new projection is 1.1 percentage points lower. In July, the fund's forecast stood at 3.5%.
The IMF has also sharply raised its inflation forecast. In April, it projected average inflation of 6% for the current fiscal year. The new forecast raises that to 10.9%.
The lower growth outlook combined with higher expected inflation points to pressure on the country's macroeconomic situation.
According to IMF estimates, Bangladesh's economy grew 3.6% in FY2025-26. Growth in the previous fiscal year was 3.5%.
Meanwhile, the IMF also projected growth of 7% for India and 6.9% for Bhutan in FY27.
The new forecast comes during the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok. Bangladesh's economic situation, its reform programme and financing from development partners are among the issues receiving attention at the meetings.

articles.title: India’s growth outlook strengthens as IMF projects 7% expansion for two years - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: India’s growth outlook strengthens as IMF projects 7% expansion for two years  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised India’s economic growth forecast to 7.0% for both FY27 and FY28 in its October 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO), citing resilient domestic demand and strong services activity. The upward revision reinforces India’s position as the world’s fastest-growing major economy despite rising global oil prices and persistent geopolitical tensions.
The latest projections mark an improvement over the IMF’s July estimates of 6.4% for FY27 and 6.7% for FY28. The upgrade reflects robust domestic consumption, favourable demographic trends and continued structural reforms supporting economic activity.
Global growth outlook remains uncertain
While India’s economic outlook has strengthened, the IMF has warned that the global recovery remains fragile and uneven. Global growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, with conflicts in West Asia, elevated energy costs and broader geopolitical uncertainties posing risks to the global economy.
The divergence highlights India’s relative resilience amid a challenging international economic environment.
Rising crude oil prices pose a challenge
Higher crude oil prices remain a key risk to India’s growth and inflation outlook. The IMF’s projections assume average crude oil prices of $95.74 per barrel in 2026, representing a 41% increase from 2025, before easing to $87.39 per barrel in 2027.
As a major oil importer, India could face increased import costs and pressure on its trade balance if energy prices remain elevated. Higher oil prices could also contribute to domestic inflation and complicate monetary policy decisions.
Inflation and current account deficit
The IMF expects India’s consumer inflation to reach 5.0% in FY27 before moderating to 4.4% in FY28. Meanwhile, the country’s current account deficit is projected to widen slightly to 1.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) in FY27, reflecting potential external pressures.
These projections suggest that, although economic growth remains strong, inflation management and external stability will continue to be important policy priorities.
RBI outlook also signals strong growth
The IMF’s revised forecast is broadly in line with the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) optimistic assessment of the domestic economy. The RBI has projected growth of 7.1% for the current fiscal year, slightly above the IMF’s estimate.
The differing forecasts reflect continued confidence in India’s domestic economic momentum, although the outlook remains sensitive to global energy prices, geopolitical developments and inflationary pressures.
Outlook
The IMF’s upward revision underscores India’s strong growth prospects, supported by consumption, services and structural reforms. However, sustaining this momentum will depend partly on the country’s ability to manage rising energy costs, contain inflation and maintain external economic stability.
With global growth facing persistent headwinds, India’s performance is expected to remain a key indicator of resilience among major emerging economies.

New Delhi, Oct. 13 -- Thrissur,
Kerala :
The DHL Group, the world's third-largest logistics company, is building a semiconductor logistics and warehousing facility in Dholera, Gujarat, close to where Tata Electronics is building India's first pure-play commercial chip fabrication plant to capture a larger share of the country's $310-billion supply chain and logistics industry.
Vikas Anand, managing director of DHL Supply Chain India, said in an interview with Mint that the company will "initially invest approximately Rs.50 crore" to set up the facility, which is expected to become operational by August 2027. Following this, it may increase the investment "three or four times by 2030, depending on the expansion plans that we have with our customers".
It would be the $70-billion German company's first dedicated semiconductor warehouse in India, though it has built and operates select semiconductor raw-material storage units at its warehouses in Gujarat and Assam.
Semiconductor logistics require specialized, highly controlled clean room standards in terms of dust, humidity and temperature levels, electrostatic-proof floors, vibration-free transportation, and high-value security and tracking standards.
The investment will be a part of DHL's €1 billion ( Rs.10,700 crore) outlay in India, which the company announced on 13 November 2025. "Out of this corpus, about Rs.5,000 crore is earmarked solely for DHL Supply Chain India, from which about 10% will be invested to cater to semiconductors," Anand added.
Before DHL, Japan's NX Group signed a partnership on 9 September with India Semiconductor Mission under the Ministry of Electronics and IT (Meity) to develop "semiconductor logistics infrastructure and strengthen supply chains in India".
The semiconductor bets come as Tata Electronics's 28-nanometre (nm) chip fab is expected to become operational in Dholera in 2027, Mint reported on 11 September 2025.
While the logistics facility is still in the planning phase, Anand said work on it began two years ago.
"About 5,000 supply chain specialists at DHL Supply Chain globally work in the semiconductor sector. Within the Asia-Pacific, Taiwan, Malaysia and Singapore are particularly strong.
For India, two years ago, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the first semiconductor mission, and investments started coming in, we sent a team from India to Taiwan, Malaysia and Singapore to learn how the business is conducted in these markets."
"When the semiconductor supply chain starts developing, the first requirement is capital equipment to set up the factories. These are highly precise and sensitive machines, equipped with tiltmeters. In India, most trucks use conventional suspension systems, so we invested in air-ride trucks. We imported air suspension systems from the US and modified our trucks to transport this equipment," he added, explaining the work that the company has already done to set up a semiconductor supply chain in India.
With this, Anand said he does not expect domestic competition in semiconductor logistics due to the specialized investments it needs, but said global competition is a factor that the company will have to take into consideration.
"Until then, Indian logistics companies will take time to learn as we replicate our global learning into India. We have a head start over many Indian companies," he added.
While being the third-largest global logistics firm, DHL Supply Chain India remains smaller by revenue than at least five Indian rivals in the country's logistics and supply chain industry-Allcargo Logistics, TVS Supply Chain Solutions, Delhivery, Mahindra Logistics and Safexpress.
As of fiscal year 2024-25 (FY25), the latest available fiscal filing, DHL Supply Chain India reported Rs.2,085.3 crore in operating revenue and a net loss of Rs.4.5 crore, according to ministry of corporate affairs filings accessed via business intelligence and financial data platform Tofler.
While Anand did not single out a revenue target from its semiconductor business alone, he said that businesses including semiconductors, data centres, electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels and other clean-energy sectors may contribute about 20% of DHL's revenue by 2030.
Industry stakeholders backed DHL's semiconductor bet, underscoring that New Delhi's growing interest in chips will only expand business opportunities for logistics and supply chain support.
"For suppliers, fabs are attractive because they provide long-term contracts, higher gross margins compared with commodity customers and provide ramp-up runways when fabs expand capacity. For logistics, the biggest opportunity may be during equipment installation, since fab equipment requires highly specialized handling," said Kanishka Chauhan, senior principal analyst at Gartner.
The need for suppliers to be located close to fabs could also drive the formation of semiconductor clusters around manufacturing centres such as Dholera.
"For most industries, being away from a supplier is inconvenient; for semiconductor manufacturing, it can impact uptime and profitability," Chauhan said. "A semiconductor fab can face heavy losses if production stops unexpectedly. A single interruption in the supply of ultra-high-purity gases and speciality chemicals can halt production. India’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth stood at 7.8% in FY26.

The IMF also revised its global growth outlook upward by one percentage point to 3.1% for 2026, while keeping its projection for 2027 unchanged at 3.4%.

The IMF warned that persistent conflicts, cyber threats and extreme weather events remain significant downside risks to the global economic outlook.

US President Donald Trump on Monday said he was “looking at” firing US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after several reports alleged that she had engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
“Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We’re not happy.”
This comes after The Wall Street Journal reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including allegedly threatening a host-country official, accepting improper gifts and services, and offering to use her influence within the administration in exchange for payment of a large credit card bill.

Infrastructure
            
                India’s Infrastructure Transformation: From Connectivity to Capacity
                प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 19:12 PM
            
                
 Building the Foundation of Growth
India’s infrastructure landscape has undergone a major transformation over the past 12 years. From transport and logistics to housing and water, infrastructure development has moved towards integrated planning and large-scale expansion. This has strengthened connectivity, improved access to essential services and created the foundations for sustained economic growth. Public capital expenditure has risen from about ₹2 lakh crore in FY 2014–15 to ₹12.2 lakh crore in FY 2026–27, supporting this advancement.                                                                                                                                                    
 A New Era of Rail Mobility 
Indian Railways is moving towards faster, safer and more modern mobility. Electrification, advanced safety systems, high-speed rail and new-generation trains are reshaping the rail network.
	- Railway budget increased from ₹32,000 crore in 2014–15 to ₹2.78 lakh crore in FY2026–27. 
- Rail electrification increased from about 20% before 2014 to 99.6% by July 2026. 
- 162 Vande Bharat, 2 Vande Bharat Sleeper Services and 72 Amrit Bharat services have improved connectivity and travel experience. 
- The Kavach Version 4.0 has been commissioned on 2,633 route km as of July 2026.
- The Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail Corridor is being developed over a 508 km route with a design speed of 350 kmph.
- Of the 1,340 stations identified under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, redevelopment has been completed for 261 stations as on 18 July 2026.
- First indigenously developed Hydrogen Fuel Cell Trainset has been launched in July 2026. It is a 10-coach train with capacity for around 2,600 passengers, running on the Jind–Sonipat section. It generates its own electricity onboard with water vapour and heat as the only by-product.
 
 
 
 Roads and Highways Connecting India
A wider and more capable road network is bringing regions closer. The expansion of National Highways, rural roads and major corridors is enabling smoother movement of people and goods.
	- India has the world’s second-largest road network at 63.73 lakh km. 
- Length of national highways increased by about 61%, from 91,287 km in FY 14 to 1,46,572 km in March 2026. 
- The length of four-lane and above national highways increased from 18,371 km in 2014 to 45,516 km. 
- The length of roads increased from 3.86 lakh km during 2000–2014 to 4.11 lakh km during 2014–2026 under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana. Since September 2024, PMGSY-IV has been launched with an objective to provide connectivity to 25,000 unconnected habitations by the year 2029.
- Under Bharatmala, 22,590 km of roads have been completed till 31 March 2026.
 Bridges and Tunnels: Engineering New Frontiers
Engineering breakthroughs are overcoming some of India’s most demanding geographical challenges. These projects are opening new routes across difficult terrain.
	- Chenab Bridge (2025): World's highest railway arch bridge, standing 359 m above the Chenab River; 1,315 m steel structure strengthening Jammu–Srinagar connectivity. 
- Anji Khad Bridge (2025): India's first cable-stayed railway bridge, in Jammu & Kashmir. 
- Pamban Bridge (2025): India's first vertical-lift railway sea bridge, connecting Rameswaram to the mainland; 2.07 km with a 72.5 m vertical lift span. 
- Z-Morh/Sonamarg Tunnel (2025): 12 km tunnel providing all-weather access through avalanche-prone terrain in J&K, improving movement towards Ladakh. 
- Sudarshan Setu (2024): 2.32 km bridge connecting Okha with Beyt Dwarka, Gujarat. 
- Atal Tunnel (2020): 9.02 km — world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet, connecting Manali and Lahaul-Spiti.
- Dr. Syama Prasad Mukherjee Tunnel (2017): 9 km all-weather tunnel between Jammu and Srinagar, cutting travel time by ~2 hours. 
 Civil Aviation and Regional Air Access
Air connectivity is reaching more cities, towns and remote regions. The expansion of airports, UDAN routes and digital passenger services is making flying more accessible across the country.
	- UDAN connected 95 airports, heliports, and water aerodromes through 679 routes, benefiting over 1.68 crore passengers as on 15 July 2026. 
- Operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 165 in July 2026.
- 25 greenfield airports have been approved after 2014.  
- Digi Yatra is active at 38 airports. The app has enabled over 10 crore seamless journeys with over 2.4 crore downloads.  
- Modified UDAN has been approved in March 2026 for FY 2026–27 to FY 2035–36 with an outlay of ₹28,840 crore, envisioning 100 new airports and 200 modern helipads to strengthen last-mile regional air connectivity.
 Metro: The Rise of Mass Urban Transit
India’s urban mobility network is expanding in scale and scope. Metro connectivity now spans more cities, while innovative systems are opening new possibilities for urban transport.
	- Metro network expanded from 248 km in 2014 to over 1,155 km in 2026.  
- Cities with metro connectivity increased from 5 to 26, while daily ridership crossed 1.15 crore passengers. 
- Kolkata operationalised India’s first underwater metro tunnel in 2024. 
- Kochi operationalised India’s first Water Metro system with the first boat launched in December 2021.
 India’s Maritime Momentum
India is strengthening its maritime backbone to support a growing economy and expanding trade. Investments in ports, waterways and maritime infrastructure are creating a more capable and connected ecosystem.
	- Major ports’ cargo handling capacity nearly doubled from 873 MMTPA in 2014 to 1,728 MMTPA in 2026. 
- Vessel turnaround time improved from 94 hours to 48.8 hours in 2025-26. 
- Major ports collectively handled 915.17 MT of cargo during FY 2025-26, increasing from 581 MT in FY 2014-15.
- The Sagarmala Programme strengthened port-led development, coastal connectivity, and logistics integration.
- National waterways increased from 5 in 2014 to 111 in 2026, of which 32 are operational. 
- India became the world's No. 1 ship-recycling nation in 2025, with its global share rising from 30.1% (2024) to 35.4% (2025) — recycling 2.99 million gross tons (GT), up nearly 60% from 1.86 million GT in 2024.
- Jawaharlal Nehru Port ranked 22nd as per the Container Port Performance Index (CPPI) 2025, published by the World Bank.
-  Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool (BMIP) has been launched on 12 May 2026. It is a USD 1.5 billion domestic insurance pool with a sovereign guarantee of USD 1.4 billion (₹12,980 crore), covering Hull & Machinery, Cargo, Protection and Indemnity, and War risk for Indian-flagged/controlled vessels. As on 29th July 2026, a total of 1608 policies covering Cargo War risks and Hull War risks have been issued under the Pool.
 Strengthening Logistics and Industrial Capacity
Infrastructure is increasingly being planned as an interconnected network supporting industry and trade. From GatiShakti to industrial corridors, the focus is on improving coordination, efficiency and manufacturing capacity.
	- PM GatiShakti National Master Plan integrated infrastructure planning across 58 Ministries and Departments using over 3,291 data layers. 
- As on 11 August 2026, 396 infrastructure projects with a total estimated cost of about ₹18.66 Lakh Crore have been evaluated through the Network Planning Group mechanism. Out of these, 256 projects have been sanctioned and 198 projects are under implementation. 
- The National Logistics Policy has strengthened multimodal logistics efficiency and supply chain integration.
- PRAGATI reviewed 382 projects worth over ₹85 lakh crore and resolved 2,958 issues.
- Over 4,220 industrial parks are mapped on the India Industrial Land Bank (IILB).
	- 272 plug-and-play industrial parks are operational across the country.
- 20 industrial smart cities have been approved across 7 industrial corridors.
- The BHAVYA scheme has been approved in March 2026 to develop 100 new plug-and-play industrial parks. 
- BHAVYA Rasayan Scheme has been approved on 24 July 2026, with an outlay of ₹3,030 crore. The scheme will be implemented over five years, from FY2026–27 to FY2030–31. 
- 7 Pradhan Mantri MITRA Parks have been proposed to strengthen the manufacturing ecosystem.
 Water, Housing and Urban Development
The infrastructure push extends directly to people’s homes and everyday needs. From tap-water access and affordable housing to urban renewal, these efforts are shaping better living conditions across rural and urban India.
	- Under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), rural tap water coverage increased from 3.23 crore in 2019 to around 15.91 crore households as on 10th August 2026.
- JJM 2.0 has been approved in March 2026. The mission has been extended to December 2028, with an enhanced outlay of ₹8.69 lakh crore. 
	- Under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban (PMAY-U), 99.25 lakh houses have been completed as on 12 August 2026. Around 96% of houses under PMAY-U 2.0 are allotted to women.
- Under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Grameen (PMAY-G), out of the 3.91 crore houses sanctioned, 3.13 crore houses have been completed as on 12 August 2026.  Nearly 75% of the houses sanctioned under PMAY-G are either in the name of women or under joint ownership.
- The SWAMIH Fund launched in 2019 delivered over 63,000 homes, benefiting around 2.52 lakh people as of June 2026.
- Under AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0, projects worth about ₹2.79 lakh crore have been sanctioned since 2015. 
- Under Smart Cities Mission, a total of 7,790 projects worth ₹1,56,257 crore have been completed as of March 2026.

BMI raises FY27 growth forecast for India to 7.5% on industrial growth
BMI expects India's economy to grow 7.5 per cent in FY27, driven by industrial activity, but has lowered its FY28 forecast amid elevated oil prices and inflation risks
Listen to This Article
BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, raised its growth forecast for India to 7.5 per cent for FY27 from 6.8 per cent estimated previously, with the second quarter (July-September) projected to grow at 8.3 per cent.
The agency cited sustained industrial growth for the uptick, even as it cautioned against elevated oil prices, expected policy rate increases over inflationary concerns and a strengthening El Niño, while downgrading growth projections for FY28 (April 2027-March 2028) to 6.3 per cent from 6.5 per cent.
“High-frequency indicators point to strong growth momentum, with our GDP tracker suggesting growth of around 8.3 per cent in Q2 FY2026/27 (July- September),” BMI said in its recent outlook for India.
The report cited industrial production growth accelerating from 6.2 per cent in Q1 (April-June) to 7.7 per cent in July-August, alongside vehicle registration growth increasing from 16 per cent in Q1 to 26 per cent in Q2 (July-September).
The upgrade to India’s growth forecast follows similar revisions by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and several global agencies after the economy posted better-than-expected growth of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of the financial year (April-June). Recently, the RBI revised upwards its growth projection for FY27 to 7.1 per cent from 6.7 per cent. The World Bank also raised India's growth projection for the current financial year of 2026-27 to 7.1 per cent from 6.6 per cent estimated previously.
Also Read
On growth drivers, the report said planned artificial intelligence-related investment by Reliance, Adani, AWS and Microsoft, along with government efforts to expand power capacity for data centres under the 2025 SHANTI Act, would likely provide a durable boost to GDP, given the longer-term nature of these infrastructure investment commitments.
However, BMI said higher-for-longer energy prices would weigh on household consumption and raise the import bill owing to the persistent West Asian conflict. The agency raised its inflation forecast to 5.6 per cent from 5.3 per cent in FY27 and to 6.5 per cent from 6.2 per cent in FY28. It expects the RBI to raise the repo rate by another 75 basis points to 6.25 per cent, even after last week’s 25-basis-point increase.
BMI has increased its assumed average Brent crude oil price forecasts from $83 per barrel to $93 per barrel in 2026 and from $71 per barrel to $81 per barrel in 2027.
Moreover, the report forecasts the consumption boost from the GST reforms and front-loading of exports to the US to fade. “Though a weaker rupee could provide some support for exports, this is unlikely to offset the impact of elevated energy prices given price inelastic energy imports,” it said.
Along with elevated crude prices, a strengthening El Niño, already responsible for a rain-deficient monsoon in large parts of the country, is likely to add to inflationary pressure while hampering agricultural and rural incomes, according to the report.
While the Indian government has implemented fuel-tax relief and targeted support measures after energy price shocks, further expansion is deemed unlikely due to increasing revenue losses and limited fiscal room, the report said.

An international student, 20, was killed after being struck by a car while kneeling in the middle of a road in Australia, appearing to pray, according to a report by ABC News. The driver, Ashton Friend, 20, has avoided immediate jail time after being sentenced over the hit-and-run death of Samia Malik in Adelaide in May 2025.
Malik was kneeling on North East Road in Hillcrest for around four minutes before Friend’s car struck her at approximately 11 pm on May 6, 2025, the South Australian District Court heard, as per ABC News. Judge Anne Barnett said CCTV footage showed Malik’s hands in what appeared to be a “praying motion” shortly before the collision.
There has been no definitive explanation for why the 20-year-old was on the road that night.
Driver failed to stop after hitting student
According to a report by the Daily Mail, Friend had been driving home from his girlfriend’s house when he struck Malik. He had pleaded guilty to causing death by careless use of a motor vehicle and leaving the scene of an accident.
During earlier court proceedings, defence barrister Jane Abbey KC said Friend had not realised he had hit a person. He heard a noise and hoped he had struck an animal or something else on the road, she told the court.
Abbey also submitted that the limited damage to his car had contributed to his assumption that he had not hit a person. Friend had checked his rear-view mirror but failed to see Malik, she said.
The court heard that Friend realised his involvement after seeing news reports about Malik’s death, which left him in a state of paralysis. Police identified and arrested him a week after the incident.
Friend was not under the influence of drugs or alcohol and was not speeding at the time of the collision, the court heard.

“I am deeply sorry for the life that was lost, the grief and the trauma caused to Samia's family and loved ones. There is no excuse for my actions, or my failure to act - and I should have acted. I do not place responsibility on anyone else; it is mine alone. I take full responsibility for my actions and their consequences. I stand before this court with genuine remorse and a commitment to reflect on, learn from and be accountable for what I have done,” he added.

Court hands driver suspended sentence
Prosecutor Frank Niemann noted that other drivers had swerved around Malik in the lead-up to her death. He said that a police car travelling some distance behind Friend had also managed to stop and pull over without hitting her.
He emphasised that Friend had not turned himself in after realising he was the driver involved in Malik’s death. Instead, police had to track him down.
Judge Barnett sentenced Friend to a suspended term of one year, three months and 29 days, with a non-parole period of eight months. He was also placed on a good-behaviour bond for two years.

Pakistan expects its economy to grow by more than 4% this fiscal year, despite rising oil prices and regional uncertainty.
Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb shared the forecast in an interview with Reuters on Monday. He spoke on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank in Bangkok.
Aurangzeb said Pakistan has secured sufficient fuel supplies and avoided shortages. He added that key sectors, including agriculture, were performing steadily.
However, the government is closely monitoring inflation. Higher commodity prices could put further pressure on households and businesses.
IMF Support Backs Economic Recovery
Pakistan has regained some economic stability after a period of severe turmoil. The country continues to receive support from a $7 billion IMF loan programme agreed in 2024.
The 37-month Extended Fund Facility requires economic reforms, including measures to increase tax revenue from farm income.
Last week, Pakistan reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF. The agreement could unlock about $1.21 billion under the Fund’s lending and climate programmes, subject to approval and completion of the required steps.
Pakistan Seeks $10 Billion US Facility
Pakistan is also discussing a proposed $10 billion exchange stabilisation facility with the United States, Aurangzeb said.
He did not give a timeline for concluding the negotiations. He said the facility would provide valuable support if secured.
However, he stressed that failure to secure the funding would not prevent Pakistan from accessing international markets.
The government is also holding talks with the US Export-Import Bank and the US International Development Finance Corporation.
Government Targets Over $1 Billion From Privatisation
Pakistan plans to move forward with the privatisation of five to six state-owned entities during the current fiscal year.
Aurangzeb said the deals could generate more than $1 billion. Around a dozen entities are in the pipeline, including power distribution companies and airport operations.
The government sees privatisation as a key part of its economic reform agenda. Selling or restructuring loss-making state-owned firms could help reduce pressure on public finances.
Aurangzeb said the government wants the private sector to play a leading role in the economy. He added that the state would support businesses and help create a stronger environment for investment.
Inflation and Regional Risks Remain
Pakistan remains exposed to prolonged conflict in the Middle East. Its reliance on Gulf energy imports, remittances and regional financing makes it vulnerable to external shocks.
Higher oil prices could also increase inflation and raise costs across the economy.
Despite these risks, the government expects growth to exceed 4% this fiscal year. Its progress will depend on economic stability, continued reforms and the success of planned privatisation deals.

Piyush Goyal urges Indian startups to expand globally as US visa restrictions reshape talent mobility and business opportunities. The shift highlights India’s opportunity to strengthen its startup ecosystem, attract skilled professionals, access international markets, and build globally competitive businesses amid changing US immigration policies.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal urges Indian startups to expand beyond the domestic market and compete globally, arguing that changing US immigration policies could accelerate talent retention, deepen innovation, and strengthen India’s technology ecosystem. Speaking at an ETSA event after attending the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting in the United States, Goyal discusses India-US trade negotiations, foreign investment, startup funding, and the country’s growing opportunities in deep technology.
Goyal believes tighter restrictions on H-1B visas and the green card program could encourage skilled Indian professionals to build businesses at home rather than relocate to the United States. He argues that India can retain valuable expertise, generate domestic employment, and increase economic activity as technology companies expand their operations and global capability centers across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurugram, Noida, and Mumbai.
“Not getting H-1B visas is going to create probably a greater thrust to the startup ecosystem. We’ve only just begun”, says Goyal, highlighting the potential for stronger entrepreneurship and innovation. He also points to the growing ability of businesses to deliver services remotely, reducing the need for professionals to relocate overseas.
According to Goyal, India offers access to highly skilled professionals at substantially lower costs, alongside domestic infrastructure, consumer demand, and a growing network of entrepreneurs. Retaining talent could also strengthen deep-tech startups working across artificial intelligence, defense, research, and other advanced technology segments. He acknowledges that India has only a few thousand significant deep-tech startups, indicating substantial room for expansion.
Also Read: How India's Semiconductor Push is Creating Opportunities for AI Chip Startups
On India-US trade negotiations, Goyal says both countries continue discussions despite changing tariff policies and differences in negotiating positions. He explains that a free trade agreement (FTA) aims to provide preferential market access rather than eliminate every tariff. India wants to secure competitive advantages for its exporters while retaining the ability to protect domestic economic interests.
Goyal also highlights India’s broader trade strategy, noting that nine FTAs cover 38 developed countries. These agreements could provide Indian businesses and startups access to markets representing approximately $85 trillion in gross domestic product, creating opportunities to scale exports, attract investment, and integrate into global supply chains.
He says the India-European Union trade agreement has achieved unanimous support among the EU’s 27 member states and expects the approval process to move quickly. Meanwhile, negotiations with Washington continue as both sides work through the legal and commercial details of their proposed agreement.
Addressing foreign investment outflows, Goyal attributes pressure on Indian capital markets partly to stronger investor interest in technology stocks in developed economies and narrower interest-rate differentials between US and Indian bonds. He also notes that India’s artificial intelligence ecosystem has yet to develop enough listed companies to generate a broader market impact.
To accelerate international expansion, Goyal says the government stands ready to support startups seeking opportunities at overseas exhibitions, conferences, and industry events. He cites Bharat Innovates in Nice, France, where 130 deep-tech startups were selected from 3,000 applicants, as an example of showcasing Indian innovation to global audiences.
Goyal urges founders to pursue international markets rather than rely solely on domestic demand, emphasizing that global competitiveness will determine which businesses emerge as long-term technology leaders.

articles.title: Vector Line Capital makes first India investment with $75 million in Tessolve - DQ
articles.summary: Vector Line Capital makes first India investment with $75 million in Tessolve  DQ
articles.full_text:
Tessolve Semiconductor, an Indian semiconductor engineering company, has secured $75 million from US-based Vector Line Capital as it plans acquisitions to expand its chip design, validation and testing capabilities amid growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure.
The investment marks Vector Line Capital’s first in India, Tessolve said in an announcement on October 11, 2026. The company did not disclose the valuation at which the investment was made or the equity stake acquired by the investor.
Tessolve, a Hero Electronix company, said the capital would support strategic acquisitions to expand its service offerings and global presence. It is already in advanced discussions to complete multiple acquisitions over the next two quarters, according to the announcement.
The investment adds Vector Line to Tessolve’s existing investor base, which includes private equity firms TPG and Novo Tellus Capital Partners.
Focus on AI and HPC chip development
Founded in 2004, Tessolve provides semiconductor engineering services spanning chip architecture, design, validation, testing and embedded systems. The company said it works with hyperscalers and 18 of the world’s 20 largest semiconductor companies.
Its capabilities include designing AI and HPC chips using in-house semiconductor platforms and design flows intended to shorten development cycles. It also operates laboratories and maintains partnerships with foundries, intellectual property (IP) providers, electronic design automation (EDA) companies and test equipment manufacturers.
“Two decades ago we started with silicon test engineering. Today we are designing and productizing complete chips for the companies building AI infrastructure,” said Srini Chinamilli, co-founder and chief executive officer of Tessolve. He said the investment would support acquisitions that strengthen the company’s offerings.
Vector Line Capital founder and chief executive Geoffrey Baldwin said increasing semiconductor complexity was prompting technology companies to work with engineering partners that can support multiple stages of chip development, from design to validation and testing.
Tessolve employs more than 3,500 engineers across 10 countries and operates nine laboratories globally, according to the company.
India’s semiconductor ecosystem expands
The investment comes as India seeks to build capabilities across the semiconductor value chain, including chip design, fabrication, advanced packaging, testing and research.
In September 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology outlined the implementation approach for Semicon 2.0, highlighting investment commitments of around ₹1 lakh crore and plans to strengthen capabilities across design, manufacturing equipment, materials, fabrication, advanced packaging and talent development. The initiative builds on the government’s earlier semiconductor programme, which had a ₹76,000 crore outlay.
Separately, Tata Electronics and Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML signed an agreement in May 2026 to collaborate on India’s first front-end semiconductor fabrication plant in Dholera, Gujarat. The proposed facility represents an investment of about $11 billion by Tata Electronics and is intended to manufacture 300mm wafers.
While fabrication projects focus on manufacturing chips, engineering businesses such as Tessolve operate across the design, verification, validation and testing stages. These capabilities are important to companies developing increasingly complex processors for AI computing, data centres and other applications.
Tessolve said it has been working with emerging foundries, outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) providers and chip startups in India, supporting them across the engineering value chain.
The extent to which the latest investment translates into expanded engineering capacity will depend on the acquisitions Tessolve completes and the capabilities it adds. The company has not disclosed the proposed acquisition targets or the expected financial contribution of the investment.

articles.title: Inflation may surge to 6-7%, RBI may need to raise repo rate by 100-150 bps: Report - bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: Inflation may surge to 6-7%, RBI may need to raise repo rate by 100-150 bps: Report  bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
India's inflation risks are significantly higher than the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) currently acknowledges, with price pressures likely to push inflation to 6-7 per cent in the coming quarters, potentially requiring further interest rate hikes, according to a report by Systematix Institutional Equities.
New Delhi [India], October 12 (ANI): India's inflation risks are significantly higher than the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) currently acknowledges, with price pressures likely to push inflation to 6-7 per cent in the coming quarters, potentially requiring further interest rate hikes, according to a report by Systematix Institutional Equities.
The report highlighted that the central bank's inflation projections underestimate the growing risks from rising input costs, elevated household inflation expectations and broadening price pressures across the economy.
According to the report, the RBI's household survey showed inflation expectations averaging 9.1 per cent in September 2026, significantly higher than headline inflation and continuing to rise.
It noted that the RBI's inflation diffusion index also indicated that price pressures were spreading across a wider range of categories, suggesting that inflation was becoming increasingly broad-based.
It highlighted that the RBI attributed rising fuel inflation largely to an unfavourable base effect while simultaneously acknowledging supply-side risks from the deficient southwest monsoon, El Nino conditions and volatile international oil prices.
The report also pointed to mounting cost pressures on Indian companies, particularly manufacturers, as evidence of persistent supply-side inflation.
Input costs for non-financial companies rose around 40 per cent year-on-year in the first quarter of FY27, alongside a 45 per cent increase in crude oil prices. Gross margins contracted by 650-800 basis points as companies were able to pass on only part of the increase in costs to consumers.
It further warned that government subsidies on food, energy and fertilisers, along with under-recoveries at oil marketing companies, had cushioned the inflationary impact of the West Asia conflict.
"As this fiscal support wanes, pipeline inflation is likely to accelerate in the coming months and add to the existing momentum," the report said.
On monetary policy, Systematix noted that the RBI's 25-basis-point repo rate hike to 5.50 per cent and its shift towards calibrated tightening marked the beginning of a new rate-hike cycle.
However, it cautioned that the latest increase might not be sufficient to contain inflation, particularly as real interest rates remained negative when measured against elevated inflation expectations.
"Inflation could surprise to the upside and reach 6-7% in the coming quarters. Restoring a real rate of at least 1% would require further hikes and a terminal repo rate of 6.5-7%, or 100-150 bps above the current 5.5%," the report stated.
The report also highlighted that the RBI had raised its FY27 GDP growth projection to 7.1 per cent from 6.7 per cent, following stronger-than-expected growth of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter.
At the same time, the central bank revised its inflation projections upwards, with inflation expected to reach 6 per cent in the third quarter of FY27, compared with its earlier projection of 5.9 per cent.
Systematix cautioned that continued inflationary pressures and further monetary tightening could create a double challenge for financial markets, with higher interest rates weighing on equity valuations while rising input costs and borrowing expenses squeeze corporate earnings.
The report also warned that the benchmark 10-year government bond yield, already around 7.24 per cent, could rise above 7.5 per cent if inflation exceeds expectations and the RBI continues raising interest rates. (ANI)

articles.summary: India's semiconductor sector sees M&A, investment surge for AI data centers  ET Datacenters
articles.full_text:
India's semiconductor ecosystem is experiencing significant growth in mergers, acquisitions, and investments. This expansion is driven by government support, a strong talent pool, and increasing global interest, particularly for AI data centre applications.
Highlights
- India's semiconductor sector sees rising M&A and investment.
- Startups raised $474 million in 2025, $228.7 million this year.
- Infineon acquired C2i Semiconductors for AI data centre power solutions.
- Government initiatives and talent pool drive ecosystem growth.
India's semiconductor sector is witnessing a surge in mergers, acquisitions, and investments, driven by both international chipmakers and domestic companies. This growth reflects a maturing ecosystem and rising investor confidence, with implications for AI data centre applications.
Seven acquisitions were announced in 2026, reflecting interest in India’s semiconductor capabilities. Five-year data from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Tracxn, and industry estimates signal this maturing ecosystem. The ₹76,000-crore India Semiconductor Mission in 2021 sparked immediate interest, drawing $25.1 million to local startups that year. Momentum surged alongside key milestones, such as Micron’s chip packaging plant in Sanand, Gujarat.
Startups raised $153.7 million in 2023, $113.7 million in 2024, and $474 million in 2025. They added another $228.7 million through early October this year. The number of first-time investors in the semiconductor industry followed a similar trajectory, jumping from 12 in 2021 to 80 in 2024. The Union Cabinet approved the Tata Group’s first chip fabrication unit in Dholera, Gujarat, in 2024.
In 2023, Indian semiconductor startups saw $14.4 million in seed-stage investment, $31.3 million in early-stage, and $108 million in late-stage investment. Two years later, in 2025, seed-stage investments rose to $33.4 million, and early-stage investment grew to $79.4 million. Late-stage investment in Indian semiconductor startups more than tripled to $361 million in 2025.
Rajan Anandan, managing director of global venture capital firm Peak XV Partners, said India is seeing the beginning of a massive semiconductor startup ecosystem. He noted that talent is the core reason, as 20 per cent of global semiconductor designers are in India. Peak XV has invested in semiconductor startups Agrani Labs, C2i Semiconductors, InCore Semiconductors, and Mindgrove.
M&A activity and AI data centre focus
A similar trend is emerging in mergers and acquisitions. Among 3,557 companies in the semiconductor and allied sectors, 68 were acquired at a median price of $33.7 million. As many as 27 M&A deals were announced over the last five years, including seven in 2026 alone. The median deal price jumped to $125 million in these deals.
One of the largest acquisitions in the last five years was Narayan Powertech, a Vadodara-based manufacturer. In 2024, New Hampshire–headquartered Standex acquired the company for $261.9 million. Japan’s Renesas bought Bengaluru-headquartered Steradian Semiconductors for nearly $36 million in 2022. Steradian provides radar solutions for object recognition.
Germany’s Infineon in August 2026 announced the acquisition of Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors. C2i specialises in software-defined multiphase controllers and smart power stages for AI data centre applications. Adam White, president of Infineon’s Power Systems division, said this acquisition strengthens Infineon’s leadership in power solutions for AI data centres. He added that it creates a new centre of excellence for digital power technologies in India.
M&A activity over the past five years is not restricted to pure-play chip designers. It now extends into companies focused on water recycling and power optimisation for silicon chips, experts noted. Sateesh Andra, managing partner at venture capital firm Endiya Partners, said there is a gradual shift towards intellectual property ownership. Indian startups are moving beyond design services to develop proprietary semiconductor products and technologies.
Government support for semiconductor initiatives and manufacturing incentives is improving ecosystem infrastructure and investment visibility, Andra said. More engineers with global semiconductor experience are now launching deep-tech ventures.

articles.summary: One dead, several injured in roller coaster incident at Georgia theme park in US  The Times of IndiaOne dead and several hurt after rollercoaster incident at Six Flags  BBCWitnesses describe horrifying moment when man was killed on the Six Flags Goliath roller coaster  11Alive.comSix Flags shares plunge after-hours following report of deadly roller coaster incident  CNBCOne dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in US  Th...

A man died after being ejected from a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, with witnesses describing a horrifying scene in which he struck the ride several times before falling onto the roof of a haunted house attraction below.
The incident occurred on the Goliath roller coaster at the amusement park in Cobb County, about 15 miles northwest of Atlanta. Police confirmed one death and said several others were injured, but did not provide details about the injuries or explain what caused the incident.
Witnesses told local broadcaster 11Alive that the man appeared to be thrown from his coaster car and struck the ride multiple times as he fell. One passenger said the incident was captured in a souvenir photograph taken during the ride.
“He was in our pictures,” the witness said. “He fell and hit the car three different times.” He added that the man’s body struck other riders before landing on the roof of a haunted house attraction.
Another couple who were riding the coaster said they saw the man being ejected from his car. “We saw it all,” the man said, while his wife described the moment as they went from enjoying the ride to screaming in shock.
A woman told 11Alive that the man had been on the ride with his son, while his wife and daughter watched from the ground.
The incident left other riders stranded on an incline and prompted an evacuation of the park. Videos show passengers being helped out of the stationary coaster cars and onto a staircase. The riders were in a car behind the one involved in the fatal incident.
The cause of the accident remains unknown. Cobb County Police said detectives from the department’s major crimes unit were investigating.
In a statement, Six Flags said it was “deeply saddened by the guest incident” and that park staff and local authorities had responded immediately. The company said it was cooperating fully with investigators and providing support to affected guests and employees.
Cobb County board of commissioners chairwoman Lisa Cupid said she could not imagine the horror experienced by park visitors and staff. She added that next of kin had been notified and expressed condolences to the deceased man’s family.
“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” Cupid said.

RIYADH: Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen’s Houthi militia toward Khamis Mushayt in the Kingdom’s southwest early Monday, as the Arab Coalition supporting Yemen’s government said it was tracking threats from drones and cruise missiles targeting the Kingdom.
The coalition said it had detected the threats and was working to counter them.
Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the coalition, announced the ballistic missile interception on X. The Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defense separately issued an alert warning of a potential attack on Abha, in the southwestern Asir region, before later declaring that the danger had passed.
Riyadh airport suspension extended
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority announced on Monday that the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had been extended to allow safety inspections of its facilities to be completed.
The airport was closed following a deadly attack on Saturday. On Sunday, a Pakistani national was killed and 11 others were injured when an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4, triggering a fire, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said. The injured were taken to hospital, while authorities assessed the damage.
Sunday’s incident was the fourth reported strike on Riyadh’s airport in five days. Coalition forces also said air defenses intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
Footage broadcast by Saudi state television of Saturday’s attack showed scores of religious pilgrims queuing at a gate before a bright orange flash sent people running in panic. Parts of the roof appeared to cave in.
Houthis claim wider attacks
The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack and said they had also struck King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the Eastern Province, as well as two facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority confirmed that Dammam’s airport had been targeted on Sunday evening, saying damage assessments and safety inspections were underway.
The latest developments follow a series of Houthi missile and drone attacks on southwestern Saudi Arabia. Khamis Mushayt and Abha, both in the Asir region, have been targeted in recent weeks, along with Jazan and Najran, which border Yemen.
The attacks have heightened concerns about the security of Saudi Arabia’s civilian infrastructure, particularly its aviation facilities, and the potential for further escalation as the Kingdom continues to support Yemen’s internationally recognized government in its conflict with the Houthis.
Diplomatic efforts to de-escalate
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan discussed regional tensions and efforts to de-escalate the conflict with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi on Sunday, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
Araqchi said Tehran was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The diplomatic contacts followed expressions of solidarity with Saudi Arabia from Bahrain, the United Kingdom, Jordan and the European Union after the attacks on Riyadh’s airport.

articles.title: Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Houthi missile attack targets Saudi capital Riyadh for third day in a row  Al JazeeraNo warning before impact: Saudi Arabia’s alert system went silent amid Houthi attacks  The Times of IndiaSaudi Crown Prince Moving Palace To Palace Amid Houthi Attacks: Report  NDTVSaudi-Houthi strikes continue as Yemen's humanitarian crisis deepens  CGTNSaudi Energy Minister says attacks testing infrastructure, vows response  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting in Yemen has said its forces intercepted another ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as the city reels from attacks that have killed at least 14 people in recent days.
In a statement on X, Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthis fired one ballistic missile at Riyadh and two towards Khamis Mushait, a city in the southwest.
All three were “intercepted and destroyed”, he said.
Residents of Riyadh reported several powerful explosions on Monday night, moments after a text message to their phones warned of an aerial threat.
The Houthis, who control Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, said their target in Riyadh had been King Khalid International airport.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the group had also sent a drone towards a military airbase at Khamis Mushait, near the Yemeni border. He again warned international airlines and travellers “against operating flights to airports” in Saudi Arabia, except in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, saying the facilities were “unsafe”.
The renewed attacks came as King Khalid International airport in Riyadh remains closed after a Houthi attack on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 others. Another strike on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11.
Saudi authorities said the airport would remain closed until this Saturday, and airlines have canceled flights. The Houthis have also struck Saudi oil facilities.
The attacks come as the Houthis fight forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government for control of the country. The Saudi-led coalition has carried out an air campaign against the Houthis and backed the government’s ground forces. The fighting erupted amid regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Speaking at an energy conference in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud said the attacks on airports over the last week have tested the kingdom’s resilience.
“The events of recent weeks are serious,” the minister said. “Our response must be equally serious.” He added that Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to diversify the Saudi economy, “must continue. Investment must continue”.
Saudi authorities have meanwhile opened an investigation into why the country’s air defences failed to stop the barrage, according to two regional officials who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity. An initial inquiry found that the Houthis first launched several drones to clear a path for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles, which then reached the airport, the officials said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles with warheads that can change direction in flight, posing a challenge to the Patriot interceptors and other systems the Saudis rely on.
One official told AP that investigators also wanted to know why the defences had not given earlier warning of an attack in which missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km, or 620 miles, to reach Riyadh.
US President Donald Trump separately criticised the Houthis but gave no indication that Washington would intervene. “Well, the Houthis are misbehaving very badly. No good,” he told reporters when asked what he planned to do about the group.
A Houthi official warned that US involvement would bring retaliation.
“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told the AFP news agency.
Al-Bukhaiti also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.
The United Arab Emirates’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Monday that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week. It also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.
Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Saturday.
US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for October 23.

articles.title: Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes  Al JazeeraZelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue  The GuardianTrump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine  AxiosZelenskyy urges U.S. to ensure Russia respects energy ceasefire  The HinduRussia offers one-day ceasefire if Ukraine holds elections, rejects Zelenskyy's 60-day truce bid  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war.
Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday.
“Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters, referring to Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Because I said, ‘You agree’. That’s why they agreed, because I said they agree.”
When pressed about the Russian strikes, Trump said, “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.”
The US president called the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a “disaster” and claimed, without offering evidence, that at least 32,000 people had been killed this month alone.
“All I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war,” he said.
Kyiv blindsided
Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel, a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said it reversed years of Western efforts to isolate Russia’s economy and would only embolden Putin.
Lawmakers from both major parties in the United States have also said the diesel decision appears to violate US law. Several Republicans have objected that it undercuts a law Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions on Moscow.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”.
But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow would not comply.
“Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.”
Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign.
“I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.
US midterms
Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from Washington, DC, said Trump has previously announced agreements between Russia and Ukraine that never materialised.
“He says he wants to protect industries in the US like farmers and ranchers, and to do that he needs the price to go down. But it seems that he thinks there’s a deal, but no one else is sure that there actually is one,” Fisher said.
The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol.
An opinion survey published on October 1 by the Associated Press news agency and the University of Chicago suggested that 65 percent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran.
Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion.
The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow.
“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

US Senator 
Bernie Sanders
 has criticised 
Elon Musk
 for spending $366 million to support Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections, pointing to the tech billionaire’s sharp rise in wealth since backing President Donald Trump’s election campaign.
Sanders said Musk had spent $290 million to help elect Trump and had since become $696 billion richer, becoming the world’s first trillionaire. He added that Musk was now spending $366 million to help Republicans retain control of Congress.
"Elon Musk spent $290 million to elect Trump. It paid off. Since his election, Musk got $696 billion richer & became the world’s 1st trillionaire. But that’s not enough. Now, Musk is spending $366 million to keep Republicans in control of Congress. STOP MUSK. STOP OLIGARCHY," Sanders said in a post on X.
This comes as Elon Musk said that Starlink’s entry into India would benefit consumers by offering them more choices, arguing that Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani would remain in business even if competition reduced his profits.
In a post on X, Musk criticised what he described as arguments by Ambani’s supporters against Starlink’s entry into the Indian market, calling them “absurd hypocrisy and hyperbole”.
“On the one hand, they say Starlink couldn’t possibly compete with the amazing low prices offered by Ambani’s de facto monopoly in India and then, in the same breath, they essentially claim that Starlink would be too strong of a competitor!” Musk wrote.
“The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” he added.
Musk’s remarks follow an earlier post on Friday in which he addressed Ambani as “Prime Minister Ambani” and accused him of being the “real boss of India”.
“Dear Prime Minister Ambani, Please accept my humble apologies for not realizing that you are the real boss of India. Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?” Musk wrote.
The billionaire has also alleged that unnamed business groups are trying to block Starlink’s entry into India to protect their market positions. The government has rejected these allegations, maintaining that the delay is due to pending regulatory and security requirements.
Musk’s $276 million push to back Republicans
According to a report by The New York Times on Monday, Musk has spent $276 million since July alone, including $158 million through a super PAC focused on Republican Senate candidates. The report identified him as the largest single donor this year.
Musk, considered a close ally of Trump, served as a special government adviser to the White House last year. His political action committee, America PAC, has confirmed the spending figures.
Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC, defended the expenditure, saying it was necessary to prevent Democrats from taking control of Congress in the midterm elections.
“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo told The New York Times.
The spending comes as Republican candidates contend with Trump’s low approval ratings and growing concerns among voters over the cost of living. Democrats are seeking to capitalise on dissatisfaction with the president’s tenure and regain control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
