articles.summary: Nepal rescuers reach flood-hit villages as at least 5 people reported missing  AP News'Massive rock avalanche likely caused Nepal flood'  The Times of IndiaFive people missing as Nepal floods damage bridges, hydropower projects in Gorkha  Telegraph IndiaVillages evacuated as flash flood from Budhi Gandaki River hits northern Nepal  The HinduNo major impact expected at Bihar barrage from Nepal flash flood: Deputy CM  ThePrint
articles.full_text:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Nepalese military rescuers on Monday reached villages hit by a flash flood the previous day, delivering aid and evacuating residents and tourists. At least five people are missing in an area popular with hikers and tourists
Helicopters and soldiers brought food and other relief supplies to communities along the Budhi Gandaki River in north-central Nepal. No deaths have been reported.
The government said an early warning allowed most people to reach higher ground before the flood struck.
Sunday’s flood followed a landslide that blocked the river near Chumchure village. The floodwaters damaged or destroyed five bridges, construction sites for three hydropower plants, and dozens of houses and farms.
Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, Gorkha district’s chief government administrator, said more than 200 people were evacuated on Monday.
High winds halted helicopter flights in the afternoon, but they will resume Tuesday to deliver relief supplies, Mishra said. Extensive road damage means helicopters will continue supplying villages cut off by the flooding, he added.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said earlier on Monday that those rescued included nine foreigners, who were taken to nearby towns.
The affected area includes popular trekking routes, and October is one of the busiest months for visitors.
Among those rescued was Chinese tourist Weiwei Zhao, who had been trekking with a friend but turned back because of heavy snowfall.
“In the morning time we heard a very loud earthquake like voice (sound) but later we know that what happened in front of our path,” she said.
Trucks were carrying food, tents, medicine and other supplies to communities accessible by road, while army helicopters delivered aid to remote mountain villages.
The Budhi Gandaki flows into the Trishuli River and is a key waterway near Kathmandu, the capital.
Videos on social media showed houses and sheds being swept away by the swollen river as it surged between steep mountains. It was not immediately clear how many villages had been affected.
Nepal is still recovering from a devastating flood that swept through the mountainous Nepal-China border region in August, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s office announced an end to search and rescue operations on Oct. 5 as recovery efforts shifted toward repairing infrastructure.

articles.title: The need to preserve the shine of Indian elections - The Hindu
articles.summary: The need to preserve the shine of Indian elections  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
The intense and unabated protests happening around and about the Election Commission of India (ECI) have thrown up a bigger question — whether the much vaunted Indian election is losing its shine. This concern is irrespective of when and how the immediate fire is doused, for the smoke could linger. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and its management have raised many questions during the last year, inviting attention, litigation and agitation. But the malaise facing the Indian electoral system is even wider. The unidimensional nature of the present noise might be drowning a larger challenge; the current scenario may only be a wakeup call.
Editorial | Rights and wrongs: On the fundamental right to peaceful assembly and protest
Elections, branded as among India’s topmost soft powers for decades, may have finally hit a phase of devaluation. The country’s enviable delivery of democratic elections, compared to dozens of countries in Asia, Africa and West Asia, which became independent around the same time, might have had the evil eye cast on them. Not only election managers, but the executive, the legislature, the judiciary, the winners and the losers in elections, as well as the wider voting community need to be play an alert remedial role in order to properly address the concerns of the electoral system.
Prime asset
Popular and credible elections have given the Indian nation critical stability, reasonable governance, post-colonial reconstruction and a pathway to development, besides the tenacity to counter external threats. The exercise of equal franchise by the sick and the elderly and by a people who are unequal socially and economically is part of India’s electoral folklore as also are the latest trends of women activism in voting. Despite rampart poverty and illiteracy at the time of independence, ordinary Indians have learned about the strength of their votes, and have nurtured a respect for the polling process. They wait for their turn periodically to place or remove candidates at positions of decision making.
The process has worked remarkably well compared to other parts of Indian enterprise. Apart from the framers of the Constitution led by Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar, who laid the seeds of parliamentary democracy, the credit duly rests on the ECI machinery, from the Nirvachan Sadan in New Delhi to the million plus polling booths across the country. The scale of the task — the 2024 national elections saw about 98 crore electors spread across India’s vast and varied topography — with the massive logistics that it entails, and the finesse of its disposal, have kept advanced nations wonder-struck. The ECI has justifiably emerged as a school for election managers from a range of countries which are still groping for ways to execute such a huge and sensitive mandate. Further, the Commission set up the India International Institute of Democracy and Election Management (IIIDEM) to impart lessons in conducting flawless elections. Younger nations look up to India’s election management as a guiding star amidst other falling models.
However, there are grey, if not dark clouds on the horizon. It may still be an exaggeration to suggest that the Indian elections are corroded but malignant encroachments cause an unsettling feeling. While elections have always been fiercely contested, with even a few social faultlines such as caste and community getting interwoven into the outcome, the results were mostly received with stoic calm. But no more. What has taken over are chronic allegations about the partisan conduct of the poll body, and aggressive grievance bordering on a rejection of the electoral results. The argument that this is part of a global decline of democratic values, and has also infected developed democracies such as the U.S., holds no consolation. No country on earth needs democracy more than India does. No country needs elections more than India does.
A different game
Elections in India have changed with the times. Ground level campaigns and door-to-door canvassing have given way to digital battles where fast moving disinformation and deep fakes are the new weaponry. While muscular assaults such as booth capturing, voter intimidation, and bogus voting of the earlier decades were bad enough, they were still limited to certain pockets. Now, the possibility of manipulating the voter database through undue enfranchisement or disenfranchisement poses a threat at a larger scale.
The influence of money power over elections, with its ability to upset the sacred level-playing field, has grown enormously compared to localised distribution of cash or goodies in the past. Expenditure reports of candidates submitted to the ECI post-election, and accounted party spends are just tip of the icebergs; unofficial estimates of poll finances are much larger. The institutional release of cash into the wallets of population segments, touted as welfare, has distorted electoral integrity, besides public finance. The Economic Survey 2026 puts the strain of such unconditional cash transfers on States at a staggering ₹1.7 lakh crore. Such brazen transactions through the front door have subverted policy and candidate level contest, causing worries to the ECI and the Supreme Court.
Post poll subversion casts a darker shadow. Wholesale defections increasingly undermine the people’s mandate for a candidate and party. Instead of reining in party hoppers, the anti-defection law has induced the bulk transfer of elected legislators thanks to exceptions allowed in the 10th Schedule. Opportunistic realignments have made a mockery of voters’ choice in the absence of a recall system. The stream of present-day lawmakers dumping manifesto and ideology and switching parties at ease, make the earlier ‘Aya Ram Gaya Rams’ in Indian politics look like timid angels. The Speaker’s recognition and symbol allocation by the ECI are critical follow ups to such mutations which have also not been free of partisan accusations.
Election management itself has got embroiled in institutional issues sparking opposition and street protests. The SIR exercise, which began a year ago, has left a trail of dust while approaching the finish line. Meanwhile, the provision of appointing Election Commissioners through a collegium under the 2023 enactment has not helped matters; and is still under the study of Supreme Court. The usual regulatory functions of the ECI such as the preparation of the electoral roll, the administration of the Model Code of Conduct, the announcement of results, and more recently, intra-organisational functioning are routinely moving into zones of contention, despite significant back up from higher courts. The distrust vocalised by polarised political entities can percolate down to ordinary citizens and create hopelessness.
Sukumar Sen, the Chief Election Commissioner for the first elections conducted in independent India in 1951, had unimaginable logistical challenges to handle, but certainly not one of trust. Today, after 75 years of experience and growing resources, while the massive logistics in elections is routine, trust has become the issue.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Anti-CEC protest fallout: Supreme Court issues fresh directions to Centre, Delhi Police
Urgent, collective imperative
Elections are by far the best organised expression of “we, the people” and hence cannot be allowed to fail. Political rhetoric is not part of the solution. The election process and its management are too precious to be made scapegoats in inter-party fights. Political parties need to do a collective and apolitical sit-down for the systemic fortification of Indian elections by building more safeguards and accountability and plugging structural and legal loopholes — basically, doing whatever is necessary and whatever it takes. The introduction of a three-member Commission to replace the single Chief Election Commissioner in 1993 had this very logic. There are multiple demands to be met: the better regulation of political financing and the menace of freebies; shielding of the electoral process from criminalisation; and dealing with the threat of AI-abetted fake narratives. Voters as well as those who are voted for must be insulated against inducements in discharge of their democratic functions. Arresting further deterioration will require collective work beyond partisan self-interest. And above everything else, trust has to be worked back into the system.
Akshay Rout is former Director General, Election Commission of India and a public policy commentator. Views expressed are personal.

articles.title: Inflation data, IT earnings, crude oil to steer stock markets this week, say experts - The Times of India
articles.summary: Inflation data, IT earnings, crude oil to steer stock markets this week, say experts  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: Indian stock markets are likely to remain volatile and consolidate this week as investors track September inflation data, quarterly earnings from major companies, crude oil prices and global economic cues. Foreign investor flows, rupee movements, US Treasury yields and geopolitical developments will also influence sentiment, analysts said.
After eight consecutive weeks of declines, the Nifty-50 gained 0.43 per cent last week, while the Sensex rose 0.78 per cent, signalling some stabilisation. However, elevated crude oil prices and continued foreign institutional investor (FII) selling could limit the recovery.
“Indian equities are expected to consolidate this week as markets balance improving domestic earnings momentum against elevated global risks. Brent crude remains above USD 100 per barrel and sustained FII selling continues to weigh on sentiment. After eight consecutive weeks of declines, the Nifty-50 gained 0.4 per cent last week, suggesting some stabilisation at lower levels, although the broader market is likely to remain selective,” Siddhartha Khemka, Head of Research, Wealth Management, Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd, said, as quoted by PTI.
Inflation data in focus
Investors will closely track India's September consumer price index (CPI) and wholesale price index (WPI) inflation figures for clues about price pressures and the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy outlook.
“September CPI inflation will be the first major domestic test this week. A stronger-than-expected reading could revive concerns over further RBI tightening, putting rate-sensitive sectors such as banking, automobiles and real estate under pressure while raising the risk of a broader drag on consumer demand.
“A softer print could ease concerns over the eventual peak in interest rates, but any relief may prove short-lived if Brent crude remains above USD 100 a barrel. Wholesale price inflation data will offer a further indication of how elevated energy and logistics costs are filtering through to producer prices,” Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, Founder and CEO of HST Wealth, said.
Global economic indicators will add to the market cues, with US inflation and retail sales data likely to influence Treasury yields and the dollar. Investors will also monitor eurozone inflation and UK GDP data, alongside developments in the global jobs market.
IT earnings to set the tone
The September-quarter earnings season will gather pace this week, with results from HCL Technologies, Wipro and Tech Mahindra among the likely key triggers for the market. Investors will look for signs of sustained demand, deal momentum and management guidance to assess whether the recent recovery in IT stocks can continue.
IT shares led Friday's market rebound, with TCS rallying more than 4 per cent after reporting better-than-expected September-quarter results. The gains helped lift the broader indices after weeks of pressure.
The sector had also faced concerns following reports that the US suspended eight IT firms, including TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant and Microsoft, from a programme linked to green card applications for foreign workers. The programme's critics have argued that it disadvantages American workers.
TCS said on Friday that the US action was not expected to affect its workforce strategy or customer engagements. The company cited the small number of applications it had made under the programme over the past two years and its focus on local hiring.
“The IT sector will remain in focus as HCL Technologies, Wipro and Tech Mahindra report their September quarter results. The sector staged a sharp rebound on Friday following TCS's better-than-expected earnings, but whether the recovery gains traction will depend on the performance of its peers and their outlook for the coming quarters,” Radhakrishnan said.
Other companies scheduled to announce results this week include BHEL, Canara Bank, HDB Financial Services, HDFC Asset Management Company and Nestle.
Crude oil and geopolitical risks remain key concerns
Crude oil prices will remain a major macroeconomic factor for Indian equities, given the country's exposure to imported energy. Brent crude trading above USD 100 per barrel could add to inflationary pressures, weigh on corporate margins and complicate the outlook for interest rates.
Uncertainty surrounding Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and regional energy infrastructure has kept concerns over potential supply disruptions elevated.
“Corporate earnings will increasingly influence sector-level performance as the September quarter results season gathers pace. TCS’s results helped trigger a rebound across IT stocks, supporting the broader indices on Friday. Crude oil remains the biggest macroeconomic risk. Uncertainty over Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and regional energy infrastructure continues to leave global supply vulnerable to disruption,” Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, said.
Alongside oil prices, investors will monitor foreign institutional investor activity, movements in the rupee and US Treasury yields for indications of capital flows and broader risk appetite.

Vijay
 said on Sunday. Vijay said his govt is trying to provide a corruption-free and inclusive governance.

articles.title: Inflation Shock: India’s Retail Inflation Climbs to 5.54% in September - Dynamite News
articles.summary: Inflation Shock: India’s Retail Inflation Climbs to 5.54% in September  Dynamite News
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: India’s retail inflation accelerated to 5.54% in September, rising from 4.83% in August, as a sharp increase in food prices added to mounting price pressures just days after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised its benchmark interest rate. The latest figures signal a growing challenge for the central bank as inflation moves further above its medium-term target of 4% and approaches the upper limit of its permissible range.
Data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) on Monday showed that the latest increase was driven substantially by food prices, alongside an unfavourable base effect. The September reading marks the fourth consecutive month in which retail inflation has remained above the RBI’s target, although it continues to be within the statutory tolerance band of 2% to 6%.
Food inflation rose to 7.74% in September, compared with 5.97% in the preceding month, highlighting the growing contribution of essential commodities to the overall inflationary trend.
The increase in food prices comes amid concerns over agricultural output, weather-related disruptions and the possibility of supply-side constraints persisting in the coming months. The rise in the overall price index also reflects the impact of a comparatively favourable base in the corresponding period last year, which has amplified the year-on-year inflation rate.
The latest inflation figures follow the RBI’s decision last week to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5%, marking its first rate hike in nearly four years. The central bank also shifted its monetary policy stance from neutral to calibrated tightening, citing indications that inflation expectations were rising and price pressures were becoming more widespread.
The policy decision reflects concerns that persistent inflation could begin affecting broader pricing behaviour, even as the RBI acknowledged that evidence of supply-side pressures becoming entrenched remained limited.
The latest data could strengthen expectations of further monetary tightening if inflation continues to rise or begins spreading beyond food and other volatile components. Economists have indicated that the trajectory of prices in the coming months will be critical in determining the scale and timing of any additional policy action.
The RBI has revised its retail inflation projection for the 2026–27 financial year upwards to 5.2% from its earlier estimate of 5%. It expects inflation to average 4.9% in July–September, rise to 6% in October–December, and moderate to 5.7% in January–March 2027. For April–June 2027, the projection stands at 5.6%.
These projections indicate that price pressures are likely to remain elevated over the coming quarters. The central bank will have to assess whether the recent acceleration is temporary or reflects a more persistent inflationary trend requiring a sustained policy response. 
The inflation surge comes against the backdrop of resilient domestic economic activity. India’s gross domestic product expanded by 7.8% in the April–June quarter, exceeding expectations and prompting several institutions to revise their growth forecasts upwards. The RBI has also raised its GDP growth projection for 2026–27 to 7.1%, from 6.7% earlier.
While robust economic performance provides support to the broader growth outlook, persistent inflation complicates the central bank’s task of balancing price stability with economic expansion. Higher borrowing costs may help contain demand-driven price pressures over time, but monetary policy generally has limited immediate influence over inflation arising from shortages or rising food prices. The coming months will therefore be crucial in determining whether the recent increase in inflation eases or prompts the RBI to maintain a tighter monetary stance for longer.

Retail Inflation Shoots Up To 5.54% In September
India’s retail inflation climbed to 5.54 per cent in September 2026, marking the highest level recorded this year as rising food prices increased pressure on household budgets.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI)-based inflation rate was higher than the 4.83 per cent recorded in August. It also marked the first time that headline inflation crossed the 5 per cent threshold under the new CPI series.
The latest data from the National Statistics Office was released a day after the Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy Committee raised the benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent to contain inflationary pressures.
Food inflation accelerated to 7.74 per cent in September from 5.97 per cent in August. Inflation in the food and beverages category stood at 7.36 per cent during the month.
Onion inflation crosses 100 per cent
Onions recorded one of the sharpest increases among essential food items. Inflation in onion prices rose to 108.09 per cent in September from 48.78 per cent in August.
Garlic inflation increased to 54.62 per cent from 43.60 per cent, while lemon inflation rose to 36.41 per cent from 15.15 per cent over the same period. Ginger, garlic, onions and lemons were among the food items registering the highest inflation rates.
Transport, personal care, social protection, and miscellaneous goods and services were also identified as important contributors to the overall increase in inflation.
Rural inflation remains above urban rate
Rural areas recorded a higher year-on-year inflation rate than urban areas in September. Based on the All India Consumer Price Index, with 2024 as the base year, rural inflation stood at 6.08 per cent, while urban inflation was 4.88 per cent.
In August, rural and urban inflation had stood at 5.24 per cent and 4.31 per cent, respectively, according to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
Garima Kapoor, deputy head of research and economist at Elara Capital, said the inflation reading was in line with expectations, with elevated food and energy prices continuing to affect broader inflation measures. She expects the RBI to maintain its rate-hike course amid persistent commodity prices and rising global yields, with two more increases possible during the current financial year.
Nirav Karkera, head of research and fund manager at W by Groww, said rates could ease towards the end of the year, although a soft base would delay a visible decline in headline inflation.
He said the inflation outlook would depend on healthy kharif arrivals, government measures to moderate vegetable prices, softer crude oil prices and a stable rupee. With costs continuing to rise and demand remaining soft to stable, policy rates are expected to stay tight as the RBI works to keep inflation within its tolerance band.

Some of India's leading names in technology, entrepreneurship, investment and policymaking will gather in Bengaluru for TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship startup and technology summit, from October 13–15. Under the theme ‘The New Tech Order’, the three-day event will examine how artificial intelligence, deeptech, and digital infrastructure are changing businesses and economies, India's place in the global technology landscape, and what it will take to build the next generation of globally competitive companies.
Now in its 17th year, TechSparks has grown from a single stage into an established platform for discussions on entrepreneurship, innovation, and technology. The summit brings together founders, investors, policymakers, technology leaders, developers, researchers, and creators to exchange ideas, explore opportunities, and connect with others across the startup ecosystem.
AI is making it easier to build products and businesses, while advances in semiconductors, robotics, digital infrastructure, and deeptech are opening up opportunities across industries. TechSparks 2026 will examine how Indian businesses can respond to these changes, develop their own technological capabilities, and compete in global markets.
TechSparks 2026 is presented by Meta, powered by PhonePe, and co-presented by Google Cloud, WOL3D, and Hostinger. HT Tech is the exclusive media partner for the summit, and will bring the conversations and developments to a wider audience of technology enthusiasts, entrepreneurs, and the startup ecosystem.
Policymakers, founders, and tech leaders on the stage
The speaker lineup includes Shri Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, IT, BT & E-Governance, Government of Karnataka; and Shri Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka. They will discuss technology policy, digital governance, innovation, and the infrastructure needed to support Bengaluru’s growing technology economy.
{{/usCountry}}
Among the entrepreneurs and technology leaders participating are Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder, Zoho Corp; Sameer Nigam, Founder and CEO, PhonePe; Dr Pramod Varma, Co-founder and Chief Architect, Networks for Humanity; Rahul Chari, Founder and CPTO, PhonePe; and Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO, BRND.ME.
The summit will also feature Mohit Bhatnagar, Managing Director, Peak XV; Ambarish Kenghe, Group CEO, Angel One; Shweta Rajpal Kohli, President and CEO, Startup Policy Forum; Ankit Maheshwari, Founder and CTO, Innovaccer; Kalavathi G V, Executive Director and Head of the Global Development Center, Siemens Healthineers; and Hareesh Chandrasekar, CEO and Co-founder, Agnit Semiconductors.
The speakers represent sectors including fintech, healthcare, consumer technology, mobility, manufacturing, semiconductors, defence, enterprise technology, and venture capital.
Three days of discussions and practical learning
The TechSparks 2026 agenda includes keynote addresses, fireside chats, panel discussions, workshops, product demonstrations, masterclasses, and interactive sessions.
Opening the event is Shri Priyank Kharge on Karnataka’s approach to technology, investment, digital governance and cybersecurity. Sridhar Vembu will speak about technological independence and the need for India to develop its own capabilities, while a discussion featuring Krishna Byre Gowda will examine Bengaluru’s infrastructure and governance challenges.
Other sessions will cover India's next competitive advantage in technology, its role as a global research and development hub, the future of enterprise software, AI adoption and technologies that could drive the next phase of industrial growth.
The programme will also look at electric mobility, including charging infrastructure, battery economics and the development of a sustainable EV ecosystem. Discussions on semiconductors, intelligent machines and precision manufacturing will examine how India can strengthen its position in these emerging industries.
Alongside the main-stage discussions, founders, developers and business leaders will have opportunities to engage with emerging technologies and the people developing them.
From emerging startups to hands-on AI experiences
A key highlight will be the return of Tech30, YourStory's annual selection of 30 promising early-stage technology startups. This year's programme, themed ‘Builders of the New Order’, will recognise founders developing products and solutions across frontier technologies and emerging sectors. Over the years, Tech30 has featured more than 500 startups, several of which have gone on to become category leaders and unicorns.
TechSparks 2026 will also introduce VibeCode30, a programme recognising a new generation of AI-native builders and showing how AI tools are changing the way technology products are created.
The summit's LiveSparks experiential showcase will feature live demonstrations of AI, robotics, creator tools, and deeptech, giving participants a chance to engage with these technologies.
ActionLabs will offer expert-led, hands-on sessions to help participants use AI to solve practical problems. Masterclasses will provide tools, frameworks and insights from professionals working with emerging technologies.
Together, these programmes will give participants opportunities for practical learning, product discovery, and collaboration beyond the main-stage sessions.
A platform for India’s startup ecosystem
Since its inception, TechSparks has tracked the growth of India's startup ecosystem, from the early rise of consumer internet businesses and SaaS companies to the expansion of AI and deeptech.
Previous editions have featured leading figures from government, business, science and entrepreneurship, including Piyush Goyal, Amitabh Kant, S. Somanath, Nithin Kamath, Ronnie Screwvala, and Alakh Pandey.
For entrepreneurs, the summit offers opportunities to meet investors, technology leaders and potential collaborators. Enterprises and developers can learn about emerging technologies and their practical applications, while policymakers and industry leaders will discuss the regulatory, economic, and infrastructure issues affecting India's next phase of innovation.
As technology changes how companies are built, financed, and scaled, TechSparks 2026 will bring together people from across the ecosystem to discuss the opportunities and challenges ahead.
TechSparks 2026 will take place at Taj Yeshwantpur in Bengaluru from October 13–15, 2026.
For the complete agenda, speaker lineup and registration details, visit https://techsparks.yourstory.com/2026/.

articles.title: Bangladesh’s Democratic Crisis and the Unfinished Struggle for the Spirit of 1971 - Countercurrents
articles.summary: Bangladesh’s Democratic Crisis and the Unfinished Struggle for the Spirit of 1971  Countercurrents
articles.full_text:
Bangladeshi-Swedish writer Anisur Rahman questions the legitimacy of Bangladesh’s post-2024 political transition, warns against the growing influence of Islamist forces, and argues that political exclusion and the abandonment of the secular ideals of the Liberation War threaten the country’s democratic future.
Bangladesh has changed governments, but has it changed its political character? Two years after the upheaval that ended Sheikh Hasina’s long rule, the country continues to confront a fundamental question about the nature of its democracy. The emergence of a Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government under Tarique Rahman has been presented as a return to elected civilian rule. Yet the exclusion of the Awami League from the February 2026 general election, continuing political divisions, concerns about religious extremism and the fragility of public institutions have raised serious questions about whether the transition represents democratic renewal or merely a redistribution of political power.
For Bangladeshi-Swedish writer Anisur Rahman, the answer is unequivocal. He sees little democratic progress in the political changes that have unfolded since 2024. Instead, he regards the present arrangement as a continuation of the political disorder that emerged under the interim administration headed by Muhammad Yunus. Describing that period as one marked by undemocratic practices and what he calls “mobocratic” governance, Rahman argues that the replacement of one political establishment by another cannot constitute a democratic transformation when the underlying structures of exclusion remain intact.
His criticism raises a question that extends beyond Bangladesh. Can an election establish democratic legitimacy when a major political force and its supporters are prevented from participating? Electoral competition is indispensable to democracy, but its credibility also depends upon political inclusion, equal rights and the ability of citizens to choose among competing alternatives. The removal of a party from the electoral process may fundamentally alter the political balance, but it does not necessarily resolve the historical conflicts that made democratic coexistence difficult in the first place.
Rahman considers the exclusion of the Awami League from the 2026 election a serious obstacle to political stability. He argues that a substantial section of the population was effectively deprived of meaningful political representation. To illustrate the implications, he draws a comparison with Britain, asking readers to imagine a general election in which either the Labour Party or the Conservative Party was prohibited from contesting. Such an election might produce a government, but its claim to represent the full political spectrum would remain deeply contested.
The comparison is intended to expose the distinction between electoral victory and democratic legitimacy. Bangladesh’s political history has repeatedly demonstrated the dangers of treating political opponents as enemies who must be eliminated from public life rather than rivals who must be challenged through constitutional means. Rahman fears that the continuation of this pattern will produce consequences far beyond the immediate struggle between the BNP and the Awami League.
An especially troubling dimension of his assessment concerns the influence of religiously oriented political organisations. Rahman believes that Islamist groups, including Jamaat-e-Islami and Hefazat-e-Islam, have acquired considerable influence over the country’s political direction. He also identifies the BNP and groups he characterises as China-aligned ultra-leftists as part of a wider constellation of forces historically opposed to the Awami League and its political allies.
These are Rahman’s political assessments rather than independently established conclusions about the extent of control exercised by these organisations. Nevertheless, they point to an important question concerning the relationship between electoral politics and religious mobilisation. When political legitimacy becomes closely associated with religious identity, the constitutional promise of equal citizenship can come under pressure. The danger is not simply that religious parties participate in democratic politics, but that the boundaries between religious majoritarianism and state authority may become increasingly difficult to maintain.
The issue has particular historical significance in Bangladesh, a country whose emergence was shaped by resistance to the political and cultural domination exercised by Pakistan. The Liberation War of 1971 was not merely a struggle for territorial independence. It also represented a demand for linguistic recognition, political autonomy, cultural dignity and a national identity that could not be reduced to religious affiliation alone.
For Rahman, this historical inheritance remains central to understanding the country’s present predicament. He traces the roots of religious discrimination and minority insecurity to the partition of the Indian subcontinent in 1947, when East Bengal became part of Pakistan. The subsequent experience of political marginalisation, economic inequality and cultural conflict eventually contributed to the Bengali nationalist movement and the struggle for independence.
Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s leadership gave political expression to this movement, and the creation of Bangladesh in 1971 established the possibility of a different national future. Secularism became one of the founding principles of the new republic, alongside nationalism, democracy and socialism. Although the interpretation and implementation of these principles have changed across successive governments, they remain important reference points in debates over the identity of the Bangladeshi state.
Rahman believes that the present political direction threatens to weaken this inheritance. His concern about the treatment of Hindus and other religious minorities is therefore connected to a broader argument about the character of the republic. The question is whether Bangladesh will continue to recognise religious pluralism as an essential part of its national identity or increasingly allow majoritarian political forces to determine the boundaries of citizenship.
The security of minorities cannot be separated from the wider condition of democratic institutions. When the rule of law weakens, vulnerable communities are often among the first to experience its consequences. Protecting religious minorities requires more than declarations of tolerance. It demands impartial policing, effective judicial remedies, accountability for communal violence and an unequivocal commitment to equal citizenship regardless of religious affiliation.
Rahman’s interpretation of the 2024 uprising is equally uncompromising. While many participants and supporters viewed the movement as an opportunity to challenge authoritarian practices and demand institutional reform, he rejects the claim that it opened a credible path toward democratic reconstruction. He alleges that sections of civil society, supported by Western interests, helped destabilise the Sheikh Hasina government while invoking the language of democracy and reform.
His allegations about foreign sponsorship and paid political agents are serious and require independent evidence. They also stand in contrast to accounts that emphasise domestic grievances, student mobilisation and anger over state repression as major factors behind the uprising. Yet Rahman’s larger criticism concerns the distance between the promises made during political upheaval and the institutional realities that follow it.
Political movements frequently acquire legitimacy through their opposition to an existing government. Their democratic credentials, however, must ultimately be judged by what they construct after that government has fallen. If demands for accountability give way to selective punishment, if institutional reform becomes a mechanism for political exclusion, or if public intimidation replaces constitutional procedures, the promise of democratic change remains unfulfilled.
This tension lies at the heart of Bangladesh’s continuing political crisis. A sustainable democratic settlement cannot be built solely upon the defeat of one party or the rehabilitation of another. It requires institutions capable of restraining every political formation, including those currently exercising power. Judicial independence, electoral fairness, protection of dissent and the prevention of politically motivated violence must apply consistently, irrespective of party identity.
The country’s relationship with India constitutes another important dimension of Rahman’s assessment. He believes that ordinary Bangladeshis broadly desire peaceful and cooperative relations with their largest neighbour, even as political rhetoric and competing geopolitical interests periodically complicate bilateral ties.
The relationship between the two countries carries the weight of history. India’s support for Bangladesh’s independence in 1971 established a foundation for cooperation that has survived numerous changes of government. Geography, trade, river systems, migration, border management, energy connectivity and regional security have subsequently made bilateral engagement a practical necessity rather than merely a diplomatic preference.
Rahman argues that forces hostile to the political legacy of 1971 continue to obstruct the development of constructive relations between Dhaka and New Delhi. He points particularly to the influence of Pakistan, Turkey and the United States, interpreting contemporary geopolitical competition through the historical divisions surrounding Bangladesh’s liberation.

articles.summary: Trump critic Ilhan Omar's Washington DC home raided in immigration fraud probe  India TodayImmigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home  BBCUS agents search home of Ilhan Omar, Trump critic and Congress member  Al JazeeraUS Lawmaker And Trump Critic Ilhan Omar Raided, Vows She Won't "Be Silenced"  NDTVIlhan Omar says she will not be silenced after federal agents raid her home  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
US federal agents raided Trump critic Ilhan Omar's Washington, DC, home early Monday as part of an immigration fraud probe, with multiple agents wearing Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) jackets seen outside the property, according to local media.
US Federal agents searched the home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar on Monday as part of a criminal investigation. The search was carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) under a judicially authorised warrant in Washington, DC, according to the US Justice Department, although authorities have not publicly disclosed the full details of the case.
The raid centres on allegations involving Omar's immigration paperwork, which sources cited by Fox News Digital said had been completed by her late father when she was a child. However, the Justice Department has confirmed only that agents executed a search warrant as part of an ongoing federal investigation. The precise allegations, evidence gathered and any potential charges have not been publicly established.
The development is particularly significant because Omar, a Somali-born American lawmaker and outspoken critic of Trump, has repeatedly clashed with the US President over immigration, allegations of fraud and his treatment of Somali Americans. Trump has publicly accused her of wrongdoing, while Omar has accused him of using such allegations to target political opponents and stoke hostility towards immigrant communities.
WHAT WE KNOW ABOUT THE RAID
Multiple agents wearing HSI jackets were seen outside Omar's Washington home in the early hours of Monday, according to local media.
A Justice Department spokesperson confirmed the operation to Fox News, saying: "Today in the Washington, DC, area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation."
HSI is the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security. It investigates a wide range of alleged crimes, including human trafficking, drug smuggling, cybercrime and cross-border criminal activity. The investigation into Omar had already attracted attention in September, when White House border official Tom Homan confirmed that she was the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation.
However, Omar had said federal authorities had not contacted her about the matter. "No, they have not," she said when asked whether officials had reached out to her. She dismissed the claims as right-wing attacks, according to Fox News. The latest search marks a significant development in the case. However, a search warrant does not establish that a person has committed a crime, and no charges against Omar have been confirmed in the reports available.
OMAR ACCUSES TRUMP OF POLITICAL INTIMIDATION
Hours later, she reassured her supporters in a statement on X, accusing Trump of using federal law enforcement to target his political opponents. "I'm ok," she wrote, describing the raid as the latest escalation in what she called a decade-long campaign of "baseless lies and smear campaigns".
"I will not be silenced," she added.
TRUMP AND OMAR'S FEUD OVER FRAUD ALLEGATIONS
The investigation has unfolded against the backdrop of an increasingly bitter dispute between Trump and Omar, one of the most prominent progressive Democrats in Congress. Their conflict has frequently centred on immigration, race, national identity and allegations of fraud involving Minnesota's Somali American community.
In May, Trump called Omar "crooked as hell" while discussing alleged fraud in Minnesota. The US President has also revived allegations concerning Omar's immigration and marital history, claims she has disputed.
Omar responded in a June 2 opinion article published by The Guardian, accusing Trump of using fraud allegations to attack her and the Somali American community. "Any keen observer will recognize the pattern of inciting hostility against me and the Somali community whenever his own failures and corruption catches up to him," she wrote.
She also accused the president of hypocrisy, arguing that his administration's approach to alleged fraud was politically motivated. Omar has maintained that wrongdoing should be investigated and prosecuted, but has criticised what she describes as the selective use of anti-fraud campaigns against political opponents and minority communities.
The dispute has become part of a broader confrontation between the Trump administration and progressive Democrats over immigration enforcement. Omar has been particularly vocal in opposing the administration's crackdown on immigrants and its policies towards Somali Americans.
In September, she introduced the Make ICE Pay Act, legislation intended to redirect funding allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection towards communities affected by federal immigration operations.
WHO IS ILHAN OMAR?
Omar represents Minnesota's 5th Congressional District and was first elected to the US House of Representatives in 2018. She is a prominent member of the progressive group informally known as the Squad, whose members have advocated policies including expanded healthcare access and changes to US immigration enforcement.
Born in Somalia, Omar came to the US as a refugee during her childhood and later became a US citizen. Her background has repeatedly featured in political attacks against her, particularly from Trump and his allies.

articles.title: What’s behind India’s “Cockroach” uprising that threatens to bring down Modi’s government: An internet joke that became a movement - ProtoThema English
articles.summary: What’s behind India’s “Cockroach” uprising that threatens to bring down Modi’s government: An internet joke that became a movement  ProtoThema English
articles.full_text:
The sight of thousands of police officers and security personnel sealing off central New Delhi, closing metro stations and preventing protesters from reaching designated gathering points hardly evokes a political movement that, five months ago, was little more than an internet joke. And yet the so-called “Cockroach Movement,” which emerged last May as a satirical response to an insulting remark about India’s unemployed young people, has evolved into one of the most unpredictable forces in the country’s political landscape.
Narendra Modi’s government is facing a mobilisation that is not led by any of the major opposition parties and has none of the traditional organisational structures of a political formation. Nevertheless, it has managed to mobilise hundreds of thousands of people online, fill the streets of major cities and contribute to the resignation of a federal minister.
The latest escalation came over the weekend, when Indian authorities attempted to prevent a major gathering at Jantar Mantar, one of the capital’s most historic sites of political protest. More than 2,000 demonstrators were taken in for questioning or temporarily detained, while the movement’s founder, Abhijit Deepke, was arrested alongside two associates upon their arrival in New Delhi.
The three were released in the early hours of Sunday, subject to a court order requiring them not to disturb public order for one year. The police operation also spread to other cities, with more than 600 people detained in Mumbai, including Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi.
Behind the clashes and arrests now lies an issue far bigger than the one that triggered the first demonstrations. A revision of electoral rolls, involving approximately 130 million deletions according to published figures, has sparked accusations of political manipulation of the electorate and the systematic exclusion of citizens from the voting process.
The government and the Election Commission reject these accusations, arguing that the deletions are part of a necessary administrative process to clean up the electoral rolls. For the movement, however, this dispute has now become its central focus.
Six words that became a political movement
The story began on May 16, 2026, when Abhijit Deepke, a 30-year-old political communications consultant from the Dalit community, posted a question on X consisting of just six words in English: “What if all cockroaches come together?”
The post was a response to remarks by Supreme Court Justice Surya Kant, who had compared unemployed young people to cockroaches. He later argued that his comments had been misinterpreted, but the backlash had already gained enormous traction online. Thousands of young people began using the cockroach as a symbol of political protest, turning the word’s derogatory meaning on its head. The insect, associated with dirt and an unwanted presence, was transformed into an image of survival, resilience and collective demands for change.
Within days, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) was created, a name that could be translated as the “People’s Cockroach Party.” Despite its name, it did not take shape as a conventional political party. Initially, it was a satirical online platform featuring mock election posters, sarcastic messages and campaigns targeting corruption, unemployment and the growing distance between those in power and the younger generation.
Its success was striking. By June, the Associated Press had reported that the movement had more than 15 million Instagram followers, a figure exceeding that of the ruling BJP’s official account. This popularity does not automatically translate into equivalent organisational strength or electoral support. It does, however, demonstrate that the movement has managed to reach a segment of Indian society that has traditionally viewed party politics with scepticism.
Deepke did not come from the centre of India’s political establishment. His Dalit background—the Dalits are communities historically relegated to the lowest levels of the caste system—gave his presence particular symbolic significance. His personal story connected the question of employment opportunities with India’s deeper social inequalities, without restricting the movement exclusively to the demands of any one community.
The generation that studies but cannot find work
To understand how quickly the movement spread, it is necessary to examine the situation facing young people in India. The country has recorded high rates of economic growth in recent years and has significantly strengthened its position in the global economy, particularly in technology, services and manufacturing. This growth, however, has not been accompanied by the creation of a corresponding number of stable, high-quality jobs for all the young people entering the labour market.
According to an analysis by the British think tank Chatham House, approximately one-third of India’s working-age population belongs to the 15–29 age group. Even more concerning is the fact that nearly four in ten school graduates aged 15 to 25 are unemployed, according to the population category examined in that analysis. These figures do not mean that four in ten young Indians overall are unemployed. They do, however, illustrate the serious difficulties in absorbing young people into the workforce, even when they have completed their education.
The problem is compounded by the way the education system operates. For millions of families, gaining admission to a good university or securing a job in the public sector represents the main route to upward social mobility. National entrance examinations are fiercely competitive and have spawned an entire economy of private tutoring services and preparatory centres. Families devote a significant portion of their income to ensuring their children acquire the knowledge and preparation needed to compete for a limited number of university places or jobs.
When this process is undermined by scandals involving leaked exam papers, cancelled examinations and allegations of opaque procedures, financial pressure turns into political anger. For many young people, the feeling is not simply that opportunities are scarce, but that even the rules of competition are not applied equally to everyone.
This is precisely the discontent on which the Cockroach Janta Party’s first major mobilisation was built. The cockroach was no longer merely an internet symbol. It represented a generation that believes it is being forced to survive in an intensely competitive environment without the protection or opportunities available to previous generations.
From leaked exam papers to a minister’s resignation
The first major battleground with the government was education. In May 2026, allegations that exam papers had been leaked for medical school entrance examinations—in which more than 2.2 million candidates were due to participate—triggered a serious crisis. The cancellation and rescheduling of the examinations provoked fierce backlash, while media reports linked the turmoil to cases of suicide. These reports require a careful distinction between allegations and an established causal relationship.
The movement took its pressure campaign onto the streets of New Delhi, demanding changes to the examination system, accountability for those responsible and compensation for affected families. Gradually, student organisations, social activists and citizens with no previous connection to the CJP joined the demonstrations. Support from well-known public figures brought additional attention to the protests.
The authorities’ response in several cases strengthened the demonstrations rather than containing them. Images of police interventions against young protesters circulated widely on social media. When prominent activist Sonam Wangchuk, who had begun a hunger strike in solidarity with the movement, was removed from a protest site, the backlash intensified further.
Modi’s government initially opted for a hard-line response to the protests, but later acknowledged the need to address the allegations. It held talks with representatives of the movement, announced measures against those implicated in the leaks and pledged to take a tougher stance on similar incidents.
The resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25 was the most significant outcome of that period. For a movement with no parliamentary representation and no traditional party machinery, the departure of a federal minister was a development that substantially strengthened its political standing.
That success, however, had a second consequence. It showed CJP supporters that mobilisation could lead to concrete government decisions. After the education protests ended in late July, the movement did not dissolve. It maintained its networks of supporters and returned with an issue that now touched on the very functioning of Indian democracy.
The 130 Million Names and the Challenge to the Electoral Process
The second phase of the protests is politically far more complex. At its centre is the so-called Special Intensive Revision of Electoral Rolls, known by the acronym SIR, which began in 2025 in the state of Bihar and gradually expanded across much of the country. India has the largest electorate in the world, with at least 960 million registered voters in the 2024 national elections, making any large-scale changes to the electoral rolls a matter of considerable political significance.
The process involves checking voter registrations to remove people who have died, moved away or do not meet the legal requirements for voting. In terms of its stated purpose, this is an administrative practice intended to ensure the proper functioning of an electoral system. The backlash has stemmed from the scale of the deletions, the way the checks have been conducted and allegations that their implementation does not affect all social and religious groups equally.

articles.title: Trump’s Targeting of Indian IT Firms Hits India-US Ties Again - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Trump’s Targeting of Indian IT Firms Hits India-US Ties Again  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
Ties between India and the United States hit another bump last week with the Trump administration freezing green card requests from eight technology firms, including those from India.
U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced on October 8 that Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini, Microsoft, and Adobe have been suspended from participating in the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM), a program that is largely used by technology companies and outsourcing firms to sponsor a foreign worker’s permanent residency in the U.S. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” Sonderling said.
The announcement came weeks before U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to New Delhi.
Indian IT companies appear largely unperturbed by the U.S. policy change. Infosys, India’s second-largest IT firm, said it did not anticipate a material impact from the PERM application suspension. The National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM), India’s IT industry body, said that Indian companies had significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas in recent years and had expanded their local hiring in the U.S. Relatively few workers move from H-1B visas to permanent residency through PERM, it said.
Ajay Srivastava, who heads the Global Trade Research Initiative, a New Delhi-based trade and commerce think tank, said the U.S. move was a “warning for India’s IT industry.” “It covers four leading Indian IT firms and disrupts the permanent-residency plans of their employees, making long-term staffing in the U.S. more uncertain,” Srivastava told The Diplomat.
“The larger concern is India’s dependence on a market that accounts for 54.1 percent of its software and IT-enabled services exports. The measure signals a more protectionist U.S. approach to foreign technology workers. India should prepare for possible restrictions extending beyond green card sponsorship,” he said, adding that Indian firms should widen their export markets to reduce their vulnerability to sudden U.S. policy changes.
India’s software services exports to the U.S. fetched $221.4 billion in revenues in 2025-26, an 8.2 percent year-on-year increase.
Adding salt to injury was a comment by Vice President J.D. Vance. Speaking to reporters after Sonderling’s announcement, Vance said: “Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
In a sharply worded statement, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said that “talent mobility adds value to both economies.” The measures announced by the United States “do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries.” Recalling that the U.S. was a country built by immigrants, the statement said that “resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive.” The allusion was to India’s British colonial rulers transporting more than a million Indians to work as contract labor in British colonies abroad after the abolition of slavery by the British in 1833.
There is speculation in India that the U.S. policy change on green card requests is aimed at showing President Donald Trump’s domestic audience that his administration is tough on immigration. The U.S. will vote in mid-term elections in November. Voters are reportedly unhappy with the Trump administration’s performance, especially on the handling of the economy, with job numbers falling short of expectations.
Last week’s restrictions on Indian IT companies, together with Vance’s comments, have added to the chill in India-U.S. relations, especially since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
A trade pact negotiated between the two sides remains unsigned despite many rounds of talks. Washington’s courting of Pakistan, which India sees as instigating terrorism against it, has not gone down well in Delhi.
Speaking at the Asia Society in New York in September, India’s Minister for External Affairs S. Jaishankar highlighted the U.S. anti-immigration push affecting the movement of Indian workers to the U.S. as among the main causes for the current strain in bilateral ties.
Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has implemented several measures to rework American immigration policy. These include bestowing more powers on officials to enforce domestic immigration laws as well as increasing anti-immigration raids and deportations. Last year, India accepted the return of almost 400 of its nationals deported by the Trump administration. Their arrival in India in military aircraft and in shackles caused a domestic outcry.
The Trump administration has also been squeezing the H-1B visa program that allows foreign nationals to temporarily work in the U.S. in specialty occupations for a maximum of six years. In August, Washington proposed a regulation to raise the fee on new H-1B visas to over $100,000. The H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, allowing American employers to hire highly skilled workers with specialty training. The program permits another 20,000 visas for workers with advanced degrees for a three-to-six-year period. Fees for the two categories of visas were between $2,000 and $5,000 earlier.
Trump’s proposed regulation was struck down by a California court in September, blocking the $100,000 fee tag. India has been the largest beneficiary of the H-1B visas program for many years.
With the U.S. narrowing the options for skilled Indian workers, the Indian government could look at asking American companies to follow the examples of Microsoft and Adobe and set up Global Capability Centers in India. These centers are offshore units set up by companies to deliver services for their parent organizations.
India presently has more than 2,100 centers employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in revenue. The Indian government is also looking to attract Indian workers currently employed in the U.S. to return home.
The denial of green cards under PERM is likely to figure in talks when Rubio, the U.S. secretary of state and national security adviser, arrives in India later this month. Also likely to figure in the agenda is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which authorizes Trump to sanction countries that buy oil from Russia and Iran. India is among the largest purchasers of Russian oil. Given that the U.S. itself is looking to import diesel from Russia, India is likely to seek clarification on the provisions of the Lindsay Graham Act should it import fuel from Russia.
People-to-people relations have always been the strongest anchor of India-U.S. bilateral ties. Washington’s latest move hits this anchor. Rubio and Jaishankar have a challenging agenda before them.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Political Crisis: When Constitutional Power Becomes Political Currency - The Friday Times
articles.summary: Pakistan’s Political Crisis: When Constitutional Power Becomes Political Currency  The Friday Times
articles.full_text:
Pakistan’s decision to impose emergency measures and Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa raises a question more consequential than whether the federal government can outmanoeuvre the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI): can the state confront a security crisis without turning constitutional authority into an instrument of political conflict? The government has a duty to protect citizens, but extraordinary intervention must be lawful, necessary and proportionate. PTI has the right to defend its electoral mandate, but political confrontation cannot substitute for effective governance. Meanwhile, the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa continue to bear the consequences of insecurity and institutional failure.
On 11 October 2026, President Asif Ali Zardari approved the federal government’s decision to proclaim an emergency and impose Governor’s Rule under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution. The government cited deteriorating security and what it described as the provincial administration’s disengagement from counterterrorism efforts. PTI rejected the intervention as an assault on its electoral mandate and provincial autonomy. These competing claims require scrutiny. Neither the gravity of the security situation nor the strength of an electoral mandate, on its own, resolves the constitutional question.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s crisis cannot be reduced to a dispute between Islamabad and PTI. Militancy, attacks on law-enforcement personnel, displacement and economic insecurity have imposed a persistent burden on its citizens. The province’s proximity to Afghanistan compounds an already difficult security environment. Counterterrorism requires intelligence-sharing, operational coordination, adequate resources and cooperation between federal and provincial authorities. If that cooperation has broken down, the consequences are serious. But a deteriorating security situation does not automatically establish that extraordinary constitutional intervention is either lawful or effective.
The distinction between Articles 232 and 234 is fundamental. Article 232 provides for an emergency in specified circumstances, including an internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control. Its constitutional proviso requires a resolution of the Provincial Assembly for an emergency proclaimed on that ground. Article 234 addresses a different situation: the failure of constitutional machinery in a province. It provides for presidential action on receipt of a report from the Governor, subject to the conditions specified in the Constitution. Each provision has its own requirements and consequences.
The government must therefore establish the precise legal basis of each proclamation, demonstrate compliance with the applicable procedures and explain the evidence supporting its decision. In particular, the relevant Assembly resolution, the Governor’s report and the parliamentary approval requirements must be addressed in accordance with the constitutional route invoked. Parliament must scrutinise the proclamations within the prescribed periods. The existence of constitutional powers does not settle whether their exercise meets the conditions governing them. That question must be answered through evidence, law and institutional oversight.
Pakistan’s constitutional history reinforces the importance of such scrutiny. Extraordinary measures have repeatedly been justified by exceptional circumstances, sometimes leaving political and institutional consequences long after the immediate crisis has passed. The lesson is not that the state should remain passive when citizens face danger. It is that emergency powers must be judged by their legal foundation, necessity, duration and results. An intervention that weakens public confidence or deepens political exclusion may create a second crisis while attempting to address the first.
 Provincial autonomy does not immunise a provincial administration from scrutiny, nor does national security give the federation an unrestricted licence to intervene.
Federalism requires accountability at both levels of government. Provincial autonomy does not immunise a provincial administration from scrutiny, nor does national security give the federation an unrestricted licence to intervene. If provincial authorities have failed in their constitutional responsibilities, the evidence must establish that failure and identify the relevant shortcomings. If federal intervention is necessary, its scope and duration must remain proportionate to the circumstances. Neither administrative failure nor political disagreement should become a pretext for abandoning constitutional discipline.
The federal government carries a particular burden of justification because it is exercising the coercive power of the state. It must demonstrate not merely that constitutional authority exists, but that its exercise is legally defensible and likely to protect citizens more effectively than available alternatives. It must also distinguish political opposition from obstruction of legitimate security efforts. A province governed by an opposition party is entitled to the same constitutional protection as one governed by the federal coalition’s allies.
PTI, however, cannot escape scrutiny. An electoral mandate confers the right to govern within the Constitution; it does not absolve a government of responsibility for public safety, administration or cooperation with other constitutional authorities. Political mobilisation is a democratic right, and questions concerning Imran Khan’s imprisonment and access to due process deserve transparent and lawful treatment. Yet a strategy centred on confrontation, ultimatums and the fortunes of a single leader cannot resolve the province’s security challenges.
If PTI considers the intervention unconstitutional, it should pursue its strongest case through the courts and Parliament while maintaining peaceful political engagement. It must also explain how its approach will strengthen security, improve administration and protect citizens. Defending provincial autonomy is a legitimate constitutional objective, but its credibility depends on demonstrating that autonomy serves the public rather than merely protecting those who exercise power.
These responsibilities are not identical. The federal government must justify extraordinary intervention; PTI must demonstrate that its opposition offers more than resistance. Both must accept constitutional limits when those limits are politically inconvenient, not merely when they serve their interests. Accountability requires different standards for different powers, not artificial equivalence between the authority to intervene and the right to oppose.
The economic consequences of prolonged confrontation are equally serious. Pakistan faces substantial debt-servicing obligations, limited fiscal space and persistent pressures involving energy, taxation and public services. Institutional conflict diverts attention from these structural challenges, delays decisions and weakens policy predictability. Investment depends not only on economic incentives but also on confidence in the rules governing public authority. When constitutional arrangements appear vulnerable to political upheaval, the credibility of economic policy suffers with them.
Security and economic recovery are inseparable. Communities affected by militancy need functioning schools, hospitals, transport, employment and local administration alongside effective law enforcement. Security operations without accountable civilian governance cannot deliver a durable settlement; development spending cannot succeed where citizens remain vulnerable to violence. The success of policy in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa must therefore be measured not simply by operations conducted or administrative control established, but by improved public safety, stronger institutions and the restoration of ordinary economic and civic life.
The immediate priority must be to prevent extraordinary constitutional measures from becoming a lasting political rupture. The federal government should publish or make available for proper scrutiny its legal justification and supporting evidence, clarify the safeguards governing its intervention, and establish measurable objectives against which its effectiveness can be assessed. Parliament must examine both the decision and its consequences. Federal and provincial institutions must preserve channels for operational cooperation, while fundamental rights and lawful political opposition remain protected. PTI should pursue its constitutional challenge through lawful means and engage in negotiations focused on security, governance and the restoration of normal democratic arrangements.
Pakistan does not need another contest in which one side’s victory is measured by the other’s humiliation. It needs institutions capable of resolving disputes without making citizens bear the cost of political rivalry. The test of leadership is not whether the federal government can impose its will or PTI can sustain confrontation. It is whether both can accept constitutional limits when those limits obstruct their immediate ambitions. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa needs security without political exclusion, provincial autonomy without administrative evasion, and federal authority without arbitrary control. The Constitution must remain the framework within which these competing responsibilities are reconciled. When constitutional power becomes political currency, the state may win an argument while losing public trust. And it is the people, not the politicians, who ultimately pay the price.

articles.summary: Assam shifts focus from bandhs to industries, says Himanta Biswa Sarma  India Today NE
articles.full_text:
Himanta Biswa Sarma has set out Assam’s industrial push, citing projects in chips, food processing and power. He said the aim is to turn investment pledges into jobs and keep young people working in the state.
- PepsiCo’s Nalbari plant has created 700 jobs, mostly for women
- Farmer engagement linked to the facility is expected to rise sharply
- Jagiroad’s first clean room is ready and pilot chip production began
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has outlined the state government’s industrial development agenda, highlighting investments in semiconductor manufacturing, food processing, power generation and traditional industries as key drivers of the state’s economic transformation.
In an article shared on Substack titled “From Bandhs to Blueprints: The Making of an Industrial Assam,” Sarma said Assam was moving away from a past marked by frequent shutdowns and uncertainty towards an industrial future centred on manufacturing, investment and employment generation.
The Chief Minister highlighted several recent industrial developments, including PepsiCo India’s ₹778-crore food manufacturing plant in Nalbari, the ₹27,000-crore Tata Electronics semiconductor assembly and test facility at Jagiroad, and a proposed 3,200 MW thermal power plant at Chapar in Dhubri district.
According to Sarma, the PepsiCo facility, inaugurated on September 10, is the company’s first food manufacturing plant in Assam and its fifth in India. Spread across 44.2 acres, the plant has created around 700 direct and indirect jobs, with women accounting for more than 75 per cent of its workforce. The company’s engagement with farmers in Assam is also expected to expand from more than 600 to 5,000, he said.
On semiconductor manufacturing, Sarma said the first clean room at Tata Electronics’ facility at Jagiroad had been completed and pilot chip production had begun. The project, involving an investment of ₹27,000 crore, is expected to position Assam within the global semiconductor supply chain.
The Chief Minister also referred to a tiles manufacturing facility in Sonitpur district, which he said would be the first in the Northeast to manufacture tiles using raw materials sourced from Assam. He said smaller industrial units in sectors such as food processing, packaging and construction materials were also emerging across districts.
Power infrastructure featured prominently in the article. Sarma said the foundation stone for a 3,200 MW ultra-supercritical thermal power plant at Chapar was laid on September 20. The project, involving an investment of ₹48,000 crore, will comprise four 800 MW units, with commissioning scheduled to begin in December 2030. Two pumped storage projects with a combined capacity of 2,700 MW are also planned, he said.
Sarma said these projects were intended to help Assam move from a power-deficit state to a power-surplus state, improving the availability of electricity for industrial and commercial activities.
The article also highlighted the proposed ₹10,601-crore ammonia-urea plant at Namrup, whose foundation stone was laid by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in December last year. Once completed, the facility is expected to produce more than 12 lakh tonnes of fertiliser annually. At Numaligarh, meanwhile, the refinery is being expanded from three million tonnes to nine million tonnes per year, supported by a new 1,635-km crude oil pipeline from Paradip.
Explaining the factors behind the state’s industrial push, Sarma cited improved security, faster approval processes and investments in roads, bridges, airports and waterways. He also referred to commitments worth approximately ₹5 lakh crore made at the Advantage Assam 2.0 investment summit, saying the focus was now on translating those commitments into operational projects.
Looking ahead, the Chief Minister outlined four priorities for the next phase of industrialisation: developing industrial parks with ready infrastructure, ensuring reliable and surplus power, providing industry-specific skills training, and promoting entrepreneurship at the grassroots level.
He said initiatives such as the Chief Minister’s Atmanirbhar Asom Abhijan and the Mukhyamantri Mahila Udyamita Abhiyan were intended to support young entrepreneurs and women-led businesses, enabling local suppliers and service providers to benefit from larger industrial projects.
Acknowledging that scepticism remained over earlier investment announcements, Sarma argued that the projects underway in Nalbari, Jagiroad and Chapar represented tangible progress rather than promises on paper.
He concluded that the government’s broader objective was to create opportunities for young people within Assam, allowing them to build their careers and businesses without having to leave the state.
