articles.title: India’s draft steel policy sets 604 MT capacity goal by 2047 - The Pamphlet
articles.summary: India’s draft steel policy sets 604 MT capacity goal by 2047  The Pamphlet
articles.full_text:
India has released a draft National Steel Policy Vision 2047 that presents a long-term roadmap for one of the country’s most important industries. Steel may not always be visible in daily life, but it is present almost everywhere. It is used in homes, bridges, railway tracks, factories, cars, household goods, power projects and large infrastructure works.
As India plans more cities, roads, manufacturing units and public infrastructure, the need for steel is expected to grow sharply. The new draft policy says India could raise its crude steelmaking capacity to 604 million tonnes by 2047, from about 220 million tonnes at present. This means the country is aiming for almost three times more steelmaking capacity over the next two decades.
The policy estimates that crude steel production could reach 531 million tonnes by 2047. Finished steel consumption is projected to rise to 505 million tonnes, compared with about 164 million tonnes in 2025-26. Per-person steel consumption is expected to rise from around 116 kilograms at present to 302 kilograms by 2047.
In simple terms, this reflects the expectation that more steel will be needed as income levels rise and more people buy homes, vehicles, appliances and other manufactured products. Higher investment in railways, highways, clean-energy projects, ports and urban housing could also increase steel demand.
The policy is still in draft form and has been placed in the public domain for comments and suggestions until October 30, 2026. This is important because the final policy may change after industry groups, producers, consumers and other stakeholders share their views.
The document is expected to replace the National Steel Policy, 2017, whose main horizon was 2030. The new plan looks much further ahead, linking the growth of the steel sector with the wider goal of building a developed India by 2047.
A major concern behind this large expansion is the availability of raw materials. Steel production depends heavily on iron ore and coking coal. The draft estimates that iron ore demand could rise to 772 million tonnes by 2047 from about 299 million tonnes in 2025. Coking coal demand may climb to 236 million tonnes from around 72 million tonnes.
Since India depends significantly on imports for coking coal, the policy gives importance to reducing supply risks. It proposes measures such as expanding coal-washing facilities, securing long-term overseas supply arrangements, improving domestic mining and using technology to improve the quality and use of coal blends.
Transport and logistics form another key part of the plan. Moving heavy raw materials from mines to steel plants is expensive and can delay production. The policy proposes a major expansion of iron ore slurry pipelines, with capacity expected to rise from around 18 million tonnes per year to more than 299 million tonnes by 2047.
Such pipelines can carry processed iron ore in liquid form and may reduce pressure on roads and rail networks. The proposal also mentions government support through viability gap funding, which can help projects that are useful for the economy but may not be financially attractive in the early years.
The draft policy also recognises that higher steel output should not lead to unchecked pollution. It aims to reduce the steel industry’s carbon-emission intensity by 39 percent, bringing it down to 1.54 tonnes of carbon dioxide per tonne of crude steel by 2047 from 2.54 tonnes currently.
Greater use of scrap steel, energy-efficient technology, cleaner fuels, automation and research could support this shift. The plan also targets steel exports of 45 million tonnes by 2047, helping India become a stronger supplier to global markets.
The roadmap is ambitious, but its success will depend on investment, stable raw-material supplies, timely infrastructure, cleaner technologies and competitive production costs. If these pieces move together, the policy could help India meet rising domestic demand while creating jobs, supporting manufacturing and strengthening the country’s position in the global steel industry.

articles.title: Trump has learnt his India lesson the hard way. Will he own up? - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Trump has learnt his India lesson the hard way. Will he own up?  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
The reversal exposes an uncomfortable truth that when energy costs threaten voters, geopolitical principles become negotiable. The question is whether Trump will now acknowledge India's argument that affordable energy and the interests of ordinary people cannot simply be sacrificed to foreign policy objectives.
ALSO READ | India awaits how Trump will route diesel buy from Russia
The American consumer comes first
Trump announced the agreement with Putin on October 9 after what he described as a successful conversation with the Russian president. Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes thereafter. A further 3 million tonnes could follow, depending on refinery conditions.
food prices and inflation, making it a politically sensitive issue before voters decide whether Republicans retain control of Congress. Trump has described lower fuel prices for farmers, ranchers and truckers as a priority.
ALSO READ | Trump’s diesel deal with Putin may be lots of barrels but little bang
New Delhi's argument has never been that Russia's invasion of Ukraine is acceptable. It is that energy security, inflation and the purchasing power of hundreds of millions of people must count in decisions about where a country buys its fuel. Trump has learnt his India lesson the hard way when opinion polls suggest his popularity is dipping and high diesel prices just before midterm elections loom as a threat.
ALSO READ | Trump strikes deal with Putin to get diesel in sharp reversal of US policy weeks before midterms
A concession that may not deliver
There is, however, a significant difference between announcing a deal and changing prices at the pump. Analysts doubted Russia could deliver the promised volumes easily, given damage to its refining infrastructure and restrictions on diesel exports. Russian export capacity has been disrupted by Ukrainian strikes, while Moscow has also imposed export restrictions to protect domestic supplies.
The proposed shipments were unlikely to make a substantial difference to American diesel prices. Transporting fuel takes time, and the promised volumes remain small relative to global demand. The arrangement may offer some additional supply, but it cannot quickly reverse the damage caused by disruptions to energy production and shipping.
That weakens the administration's economic case for taking a politically costly decision that appears to benefit Putin. If the relief for American consumers proves modest, the diplomatic and legislative backlash could outlast any immediate price benefit.
The legal battle could complicate India's case
Having learnt that people take precedence over geopolitics, will Trump now acknowledge India's long-held concerns over oil? The biggest obstacle to any American concession to India may now be Trump's own Congress.
On October 11, seven senators, including Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, urged the administration to reverse the decision. Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden also signed the statement, arguing that the 2022 ban on Russian energy imports was intended to prevent American money from financing Putin's war. They accused the administration of failing to consult Congress or provide the explanation required by law.
Tillis went further, saying there was a legitimate case that Trump was not following the law. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick has separately vowed to force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases. The opposition is particularly awkward for Trump because the sanctions legislation signed in September, named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, allows tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.
However, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insists the administration has sufficient legal authority to proceed. The Treasury has temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7, 2027, for fuel already loaded onto tankers by the specified deadline. But whether that exemption can withstand congressional scrutiny is a separate question from whether the administration believes it is justified.
If Washington needs a special legal interpretation or a narrow exemption to buy Russian diesel, it will be harder to argue that India's purchases must automatically attract punitive measures. Yet the reverse is also possible -- congressional opposition could push Trump towards a tougher public stance on sanctions, even as his administration seeks flexibility for itself.
Will India get a carve-out?
India is watching how Washington structures the exemption. ET reported today that India was reviewing the implications of Trump's announcement, with officials examining whether the US could create a specific concession for its own purchases without formally violating the Russia and Iran Sanctions Act. The administration has not reached a conclusive decision on a waiver for India, despite a September 30 conversation between Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
For India, the stakes go beyond the immediate tariff bill. Energy purchases from Russia have provided an additional source of supply and helped Indian refiners manage costs. Some Russian crude is processed in India and the resulting refined products, including diesel, are exported to international markets. That creates a further complication for Washington. Former US diplomat Stephen Mull told The Times of India that India has its own leverage because some of the Russian crude it buys is refined into diesel that subsequently reaches American markets.
Mull argued that India has options to respond if sanctions are imposed and that Trump would have to factor those possibilities into his calculations. Retaliation could deepen the damage to a bilateral relationship already strained by trade negotiations and disagreements over Washington's approach to Pakistan.
Washington may distinguish between crude oil purchases and a temporary arrangement involving diesel already loaded onto ships. That argument could matter legally but won't erase the sheer political inconsistency.
The hard lesson Trump may still refuse to acknowledge
Trump's decision does not necessarily mean he would now accept India's argument. He could insist that America's arrangement is temporary, narrowly defined and designed to address an exceptional supply crisis. He could also return to a harder sanctions policy once the immediate pressure on fuel prices eases after midterms.
If fuel prices remain high, the administration will face pressure to find more supplies regardless of their origin. If prices fall, Trump may have greater room to restore restrictions and maintain pressure on countries buying Russian energy. Either way, the principle guiding policy appears less absolute than Washington previously suggested.
Trump need not endorse India's entire position on Russia to acknowledge that energy security cannot be judged by one standard for Washington and another for New Delhi. But with Republicans and Democrats questioning his diesel deal, a waiver of any sort for India may become politically harder to deliver.

articles.title: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar says researchers have started smoking, believing AI will cure cancer - India Today
articles.summary: Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar says researchers have started smoking, believing AI will cure cancer  India TodayPalantir CTO says some AI researchers are taking up smoking because they expect AI to cure cancer  Business InsiderTranscript: Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir, on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 11, 2026  CBS NewsPalantir CTO calls Silicon Valley’s faith in AI a ‘mass psychosis’  ET Enterprise AIPalantir CTO Says Some ...
articles.full_text:
The AI industry is confident that AI will cure cancer. How confident? According to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar, some AI researchers have started smoking in an effort to go all-in on the technology.
AI will cure cancer. This is something that you may have heard from many in Silicon Valley, be it Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis or Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. But sometimes, words are not enough, or so it seems. Palantir’s chief technology officer Shyam Sankar says that AI researchers have started to smoke just to show how confident they are in the technology to cure cancer.
The Palantir CTO said that researchers were now so confident in AI that they had started smoking. “So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI,” Shyam Sankar told CBS. "I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I will—I'm showing you my chips are all in." Perhaps, the researchers think that there is no better way of showing faith in AI than to indulge in something that could cause them cancer – hopefully AI finds that cure before things get serious.
We have seen progress when it comes to AI finding a cure for cancer. In August, Moderna and Merck reported strong Phase 3 trial data for an mRNA melanoma vaccine which was designed with the help of AI. Days earlier, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said AI would find cures for most diseases, including cancers, within 5 to 15 years, a view that also drew support from Elon Musk. Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis has made similar arguments in recent years.
Machine God of AGI
Although Sankar claimed that this was just one incident among many where those working in Silicon Valley had started to consider AGI, or artificial general intelligence, as almost a god. "Many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine God of AGI,” said.
Though Shyam Sankar made it clear that such cases felt more of “mass psychosis” and “social delusion.” The Palantir CTO added that this might be “getting in the way of actually what is happening with AI.”
At the same time, Sankar discussed the two central arguments in the AI industry. One where AI “is going to end humanity,” and the other where it may create a “utopia.” According to the Palantir CTO, both cases have one similarity. “So at first blush, this seems contradictory, but it has one thing in common, which is that you, as a human, have no agency,” he added.
Shyam Sankar pointed out that no matter the outcome, it seems that the future will depend on what the “machine god” decides, and not what you may want as a human. “The machine god is going to decide the future, and only perhaps a small number of us can try to avoid the horrible outcome,” he said.
However, Sankar believes that we still have ample control and agency to dictate how AI is used in the future. “And I think it obfuscates the more profound reality that we have a huge amount of human agency over how we're going to use this technology to deliver the outcomes the American people expect,” he noted.

CHENNAI : Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on Sunday inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for various development projects worth over ₹13,000 crore across Tamil Nadu. The initiatives included those in the road and rail transport and petroleum sectors.
The PM, along with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for the developments projects at an event held at the IIT Madras.
The projects include those in National Highways worth around ₹3,700 crore, initiatives in the Chennai Port, Kamarajar Port and V O Chidambaranar Port and Amrit railway stations. He also dedicated to the nation, the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre (SGBC) at IIT Madras.
Focusing on the strategic modernization of maritime logistics, the Prime Minister announced that the nation’s port infrastructure is being heavily bolstered to push the shipping sector to unprecedented heights, with Tamil Nadu playing a central role. He highlighted a recent landmark decision to invest approximately 17,000 crore rupees to transform Thoothukudi’s VOC Port into a World-Class Mega Container and Green Energy Hub, capable of accommodating ultra-large container vessels. “This will help Tamil Nadu become a global hub for industry and transport,” asserted Shri Modi.
Highlighting the operational successes of this maritime focus, the Prime Minister pointed out that both the speed and efficiency of Indian ports have drastically improved in recent years. He noted that significantly reducing ship turnaround times by half has allowed domestic products to reach global markets much faster than ever before. “Because of this, India’s products as well are able to reach global markets faster than before,” observed Shri Modi.
Earlier, PM Modi inaugurated the Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch of Phase II of the Chennai Metro Rail Project, built at a cost of around ₹4,900 crore.
PM Modi and CM Vijay together flagged off the new services and travelled on the Metro train. The new services are covered under Corridor four of Phase two of the Metro Rail project. In the newly inaugurated stretch, there are a total of 11 elevated Metro Stations covering approximately 15 km.
Turning to the blue economy, the Prime Minister underscored the vital role of fishermen in the nation’s Ocean Economy vision. He detailed that thousands of crores have been approved for Tamil Nadu through the PM Matsya Sampada Yojana and other schemes to upgrade fishing harbors, develop landing centers, and improve cold chain facilities. . “Help has also been provided to purchase transport vehicles to keep fish fresh,” noted Shri Modi.
Elaborating on the targeted support provided to coastal communities, the Prime Minister listed several key interventions, including the modernization of the Chennai Fishing Harbour and the development of a ‘Sea-weed Park’ in the state. “Through the Kisan Credit Card, working capital is now also easily available to fishermen,” affirmed Shri Modi.
Celebrating the tangible results of these targeted maritime policies, the Prime Minister proudly announced that national fish production has increased rapidly, driving seafood exports to their highest ever levels in terms of both quantity and value last year. “This is also improving the lives of our fishermen families and people in coastal communities,” asserted Shri Modi.
Concluding his address with a unified vision for the future, the Prime Minister pledged the absolute, unwavering commitment of the central government to assist Tamil Nadu in reaching continuous new heights of prosperity. He called for a collective effort to realize the grand vision of a developed nation by first ensuring a fully developed Tamil Nadu, offering his best wishes for the success of all the newly launched projects. “Together, we will realize the resolve of a Viksit Bharat through a Viksit Tamil Nadu,” affirmed Shri Modi.

articles.title: It’s time for Pakistanis to ditch the siege mentality - Ucanews
articles.summary: It’s time for Pakistanis to ditch the siege mentality  Ucanews
articles.full_text:
Activists hold placards as they march to mark National Minorities Day in Lahore, Pakistan, on Aug. 11, 2021. (Photo: AFP)
I have known Christians since my childhood in Pakistan’s southern port city of Karachi. Most of them toiled in low-paid jobs like cleaning and were looked down upon.
During my secondary school time, I befriended some Christian boys. Some of them were extremely bright students: very courteous, gentle, and humble. I would often wonder why they deserved such an attitude despite being some of the finest souls in the entire school.
I asked one of my teachers, who advised me to ignore the shameful attitude and derogatory remarks that came from kids who were not mature enough.
During the mid-1990s, when I joined a school as a teacher while still studying at the University of Karachi, I came across an Ahmadi teacher who was highly educated.
All teachers respected her until, somehow, it was revealed that she was an Ahmadi.
The entire school staff summoned an emergency meeting, demanding that her utensils and glass be separated.
This convinced me that even education cannot help wipe out hatred and religious bigotry.
These are not isolated incidents. Non-Muslims in Pakistan are routinely discriminated against, ridiculed and held in contempt.
And it is not only scholars, intellectuals, politicians and journalists who are contemptuous towards them — even a judge thought the name of Hindu people was so impure that he did not want to pollute his tongue by uttering their names.
Such bigotry enables hate-mongers to attack Christian churches and settlements, abduct Hindu girls to forcibly convert them and marry them, and target the Ahmadi community.
Nations and states honor people who have done tremendous service for them. Unfortunately, the case of Pakistan is totally different.
For instance, the country’s Christian minority played an important role in the struggle for Pakistan, but they were rewarded with vitriolic attacks and outright discrimination.
In colonial India, the Indian National Congress was far more powerful politically than the All India Muslims League. The former wanted a united India after the departure of the British, and the latter wanted its division into Hindu and Muslim majority states.
The League was not popular even in Muslim-majority areas of what is present-day Pakistan during the 1930s and early 1940s.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, picked Pothan Joseph — a bright Christian journalist who started or developed 26 different newspapers, including the Hindustan Times, the Indian Express and the Deccan Herald — as first editor of the daily Dawn to advance the cause of Pakistan’s creation.
Suffrage was limited in India. However, legislative assemblies of that time had representatives from different religious communities. Punjab was dominated by the Unionist Party, an organization that was not initially comfortable with the idea of Pakistan. Many of its members were sympathetic to the Congress Party.
So, it was difficult to get any breakthrough over the question of Pakistan’s creation in the assembly. However, Dewan Bahadur S.P. Singha, Cecil Gibbon and Fazal Elahi, three Christian MPs, threw their support behind the League, helping it secure the 91-vote mandate in the assembly.
But within a year, the country rewarded them in an ungrateful way by passing the Objective Resolution, establishing a constitutional theocracy in the country, relegating Christian and other minorities to the status of second-class citizens, who cannot make it to the highest and senior positions in the state.
Despite this, the community continued serving society by playing an effective role in health and other departments.
However, the Islamist dictator General Zia ul Haq further paved the way for minorities' persecution by coming up with more stringent laws, including the blasphemy law, that targeted the Christian community and many other innocent people.
Using this law as an excuse, Christian settlements were attacked and burned. Attacks in Joseph Colony, Lahore, Gojra, and Faisalabad could be cited as examples.
The law made it extremely difficult for Christians to defend their religion in debates and discussions against the vitriolic attacks that are routinely carried out by the religious right and ordinary Muslims.
The case of Asia Bibi, who spent years in jail for countering the verbal attacks carried out by her co-workers, is a glaring example.
The Ahmadi community also played an important role, with one of its top leaders, Sir Zafar Ullah Khan, convincing politicians in Punjab to side with the League. Khan also served on international bodies like the United Nations and the International Court of Justice, boosting the soft image of the Islamic Republic. Military officers of this community also played an important role during the wars of 1965 and 1971, demonstrating extraordinary bravery.
Dr Abdus Salam, the only Pakistani Nobel Prize winner in science, was also from the same community. He declined lucrative offers in Europe, coming back to serve the country and helping establish scientific institutions. But he was deeply disappointed after his people were declared non-Muslims in 1974.
Ahmadis are today a pariah in the Islamic Republic and are routinely persecuted for their faith.
Sections of Dalit or formerly untouchable Hindus felt more comfortable with Jinnah than Mahatma Gandhi, whom they considered a hypocrite. But Pakistani society and the political elite also disappointed them by passing the Objective Resolution, forcing the first law minister of the country, Jogendra Nath Mandal, to leave the Islamic Republic.
Sections of the Hindu population were also targeted during the 1971 war in erstwhile East Pakistan. The remaining now face the specter of forced conversion. Terrorists and militant groups also targeted minorities. Attacks on churches, Ahmadi mosques and individual Sikhs could be cited as examples.
Apart from targeting minorities, Pakistani society also unleashed a torrent of smear campaigns against those Pakistanis known globally; Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai, human rights defender Asma Jahangir, Imaan Mazari, Abdul Sattar Edhi and Hadi Chatta are among those who were declared foreign agents.

articles.full_text:
At least 139 migrants, including 15 children, have died and 84 remain missing after an overcrowded boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti while carrying more than 300 people towards Yemen, the United Nations migration agency said on Sunday.
The boat was carrying 305 people, most of them Ethiopians, when it sank near Guhere, off Djibouti’s eastern coast, in the Gulf of Aden during the night of October 8-9, according to the international organisation for migration (IOM). At least 82 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals.
“Survivors told me that the boat started to sink backwards as soon as they got in it,” Alexandre Coissac, IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti, said, describing the incident as a “devastating loss of life”.
The agency initially reported 109 deaths and 116 people missing, but revised the toll to 139 dead and 84 missing after more bodies were recovered. The official count may rise further, as some bodies buried by migrants themselves have yet to be verified by authorities, Coissac told the Associated Press.
Djiboutian authorities continued search and rescue operations, while IOM teams provided emergency assistance. 
The agency said it was assisting 64 survivors at a migrant centre in the coastal town of Obock.
The crossing from the Horn of Africa to Yemen via the Bab al-Mandeb strait is a popular but dangerous route for migrants seeking jobs and safety in Gulf countries. The narrow waterway separates Djibouti and Yemen, but the journey carries significant risks amid conflict and instability across the region.
“Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East,” the IOM said.
Coissac said 150 people aboard the boat had previously been turned back from Yemen but had attempted the crossing again.
The agency recorded more than 20,000 incoming movements from Ethiopia to Djibouti since September 10. In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the sea route to Yemen, while the number attempting the journey rose by 18%, according to the IOM.
The latest disaster follows a shipwreck in March 2026 that left nine people dead and 45 missing.
IOM director general Amy Pope urged governments and donors to expand support for search and rescue operations and create safer migration routes.
“No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives.”
